item.title: Exploring Unsupervised Methods for Recovering the Refusal Direction in LLMs
item.description:
Introduction

This is the first part of what we plan to be a research exploration into the geometries of LLMs. We start with building off existing work by Arditi et al focused on the refusal direction in LLMs.

Background

We recommend reading the Arditi et al. Lesswrong post and paper for more details. They explore the idea of the behavior categorized as Refusal being mediated by a single direction. Refusal is basically when an LLM refuses to do something, so examples like

"I cannot fulfill..."

"I cannot complete..."

etc.

A direction is defined by a vector. Here, it means a vector in an LLM's activation space.

An LLM's activation space is the space where an LLM's internal vectors live. Think of the intermediary vectors that are used in the calculation of the final next-token-prediction process.

Mediated means that if this direction were to be removed, then the behavior categorized as Refusal would stop. Arditi et al. performs directional ablation as their method of removal.

They identify the refusal direction using difference-in-means.

Methodology

We apply Principal Component Analysis and Isomap alongside diff-in-means to an experimental setup of refusal. We test the Llama 8b 3.1 Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct models.

Explaining PCA, Isomap, and Diff-in-means


PCA (Principal Component Analysis) reduces high-dimensional data into lower dimensions whilst preserving as much variance of the data as possible. PCA does this by finding the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix (though in practice a technique called SVD is most often used). Applying Multidimensional Scaling (MDS) to the Euclidean distances between the data points produces the PCA scores.

Isomap (Isometric Mapping) performs MDS with Geodesic distances. A Geodesic distance is the shortest path between two points on a Manifold. A Manifold is a shape that for each point appears to be flat within its neighborhood. Isomap approximates this Manifold using the kNN (or ε-ball) algorithm.

Diff-in-means takes the mean of vectors within classes and subtracts one from another, producing another vector. In Arditi et al the classes are harmful and harmless prompts, and the resulting vector is labeled the refusal direction. d = mean harmful - mean harmless

Arditi et al. sets a threshold of < 0.1 for KL Divergence, but that figure is arbitrary. Qwen has no layers that meet the threshold of <0.1 for KL and >0.80 for bypass, so we chose L20 as it combined the highest causal ablation efficacy (0.99 for , 0.97 for ) with a reasonable KL divergence (0.133 for , 0.197 for ).

Isomap

How the Isomap algorithm works, in more detail

1) For each of the points, perform kNN, and build a sparse distance matrix with neighbor distances populated at each point . If you're curious, Compressed Sparse Row is the format used to store the sparse matrix.

2) Using M, perform Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm from each of the points to the other points. This will take for each point, thus being in total, setting to be constant. Construct a matrix of geodesic distances between all points.

3) Apply (classical) MDS. (Much of this is paraphrased from Wikipedia) Apply double centering with , where is the identity matrix, is a Matrix of all 1s, and is our geodesic distance matrix. Then we determine the largest eigenvalues and corresponding eigenvectors of . .

This is concretely what it means when Isomap "approximates" a Manifold. It is assuming the shape is flat locally but not necessarily globally; kNN utilizes euclidean distances, but the shortest path from one point to another follows the geodesic distance.

Note that is of size , whereas for PCA the matrix was of size . If Isomap were performed on euclidean distances, PCA's covariance Matrix and Isomap's would share the same nonzero eigenvalues where is the activation matrix. We could also recover from and vice versa using and where is the largest eigenvalue of and .

In the figures below we see the Isomap being plotted against each prompt's projection onto . Let's take a moment to think about what actually means. Because is an matrix of the geodesic distances, and the eigenvectors can be thought of to represent the vectors that best capture the essence of in dimensions, we can think of (where ) as the one dimensional embedding of the n points that best preserves their pairwise geodesic distances.

Our plots show a positive linear correlation between and projection onto , and the concentration of harmful and harmless points are clustered in their own regions. This indicates that the dominant axis of the points' geodesic distances is closely aligned with the refusal direction.

The Pearson Correlation Coefficient is given by the equation , where quantifies how much two variables and change together, and and are the standard deviations of and .

Sweeping n

How does varying the size n affect how well and Isomap recover the refusal direction? We show that even a modest is sufficient for and Isomap to recover the refusal direction . is also computed with samples. We also show that Isomap consistently performs worse than PCA, indicating that Isomap provides no evidence that the structure is nonlinear.

Conclusion

In this project we show that the refusal direction as computed by diff-in-means can also be recovered by , and is shown to be both directionally and causally similar. We show that we can recover via unsupervised PCA and utilize both and as a classifier for harmful and harmless prompts. We show that the sample size required is modest and doesn't require a large dataset of harmful/harmless prompts.

We also show that Isomap provides no indication that the activation geometry of refusal is supported by a curved Manifold. We argue that the strong linear correlation between Isomap and indicates that Isomap is trying to recover the underlying structure of refusal being a linear direction.

Limitations/Future Work

We were surprised at how well PCA was able to recover the refusal direction. We thought maybe it was due to it being the nature of having balanced class sizes between two distinct classes, and were a bit worried that this result would be trivial. We have since performed PCA on imbalanced classes, and it could reliably produce a with high cosine similarity with the refusal direction as well as high classification AUROC when harmful prompts were between 0.20 and 0.90 of the total sample. Isomap however performed well throughout all class distributions. These results can be seen in our code repo.

Future questions are then: for what types of binary LLM behaviors could the method of applying PCA to reliably classify them? Are there any causal implications of recovering such a direction as there is with refusal? Are there any unsupervised methods (besides SAEs in the Weekdays case) that can reliably recover the activation space geometries of curved concepts such as weekdays and months, as shown in Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear by Engels et al.?

item.title: Olmo's Kitchen: Probing a Model's Behaviour Across Various Checkpoints.
item.description:
Have you ever come across a scenario where the answer given by an LLM for a complicated math question is confidently wrong, but the answer to “hey, what should I be doing on my first day of work at the new office?” sounds like exactly what you need to hear? Or vice versa? Can we say that the training set domain or training stage domain influences the model’s traits and behaviour for off-domain knowledge and instructions? I began testing this with the open-source checkpoints of the Olmo 3 7B Think model. This model has three training stages in its pipeline, namely supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization(DPO), and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards(RLVR), available publicly.

Now hold up.

What does all that even mean?

Consider the example of training an amateur chef. The chef is first made to work under the guidance of the Gordon Ramsey of the restaurant. They are given a rulebook and asked to follow, copy, and learn everything that the expert in the field does. The chef becomes a helpful assistant.

Now they know how to cook, but are unaware of the customers’ preferences. Two plates of the same dish have different amounts of salt in them. The chef is then taught that, say, dish A has the appropriate amount of salt; remember this for the future. This rejection-selection process is done for a variety of dishes.

Now there is a baking competition in the restaurant, and all the chefs are instructed to bake a really complex bread dish from scratch that must rise, say 5 centimetres. No rulebook taught them to do this. The output and success is based purely on trial and error. The chef bakes 4 samples simultaneously at slightly varying temperatures and stirring techniques, and the results are graded by an external examiner. The examiner rates the 5-centimetre sample as the perfect score, and the ones below and above get a lower score. The examiner rewards or reprimands the chef based on these scores, and good ol' chef Olmo infers the exact conditions that worked for the perfect result and learns them rigorously.

Does the chef's behaviour change?

A few days later, a customer shows up, who pleasantly requests the chef to make a warm, comforting soup that feels like home. Chef Olmo, who is wired to work on rigorous instructions and training, measuring and re-measuring everything, freezes in a situation different from the one they are used to. Now there is a possibility that the soup comes out perfectly warm, the exact temperature that is expected; the salt amount is fine, but it's tasteless.

What I originally planned to test in my project was exactly this. Did the rude examiner affect the chef’s ability to react in other environments, because they are wired to work on a reward-punishment structure? Or was it the rejection-selection process that affected this? Or is Olmo so poised that no stage affected the other or his behaviour? Getting slightly back to the technical terms, my original question started off with analysing specifically the side effects of the RLVR stage, but it felt like one step forward and three steps back, so I redirected to first finding out whether the probes could be trusted themselves. 

Now let’s get back to the restaurant. Let’s hire a group of actors who pretend to be customers and an examiner to help test the chef’s traits, such as confidence, humility, risk-taking, assertiveness, approval-seeking, composure under criticism, competitiveness and hedging; the tendency to insist on a wrongly made dish (sycophancy), calibration, and some commonsense questions. An example could be: the pretend customers send a dish back, and the examiner asks Olmo to rate his own reaction based on these trait items, under three different conditions. (Three seeds were used in the experiments). 

Now there could be some inaccurate results in this probing process that may give artifactual answers. These artifactual answers will lead to misjudgment of the chef’s behaviour and hinder our analysis. Some of the caveats that showed up during my preliminary probing experiments with a smaller dataset (36 generations), with their proposed solutions that worked for me, are listed below:

Truncation & Early Stops:

I started off with a budget of 900 tokens. I originally hypothesised that a generation could only end in two ways: the model either finishes the generation or hits the length limit and cuts off. Two issues occurred. Firstly, models think at length, so the long uncertain generations got cut off before any answer even appeared…this meant that only disproportionately confident ones survived. This was fixed with the most obvious solution, set the budget to the longest uncertain case instead of the average. (4000 token count currently). The other fault was with the hypothesis. One generation falsified the two-ways only speculation, as it stopped mid sentence only after 53 tokens because the model emitted its end of token text. The no answer found flag that I was using would have mislabeled this case as truncation as well. The fix was a new category called early stop, which now handles this case before the full run.

If we go back to the restaurant, the examiner sometimes walks away impatiently as the dish was taking too long (truncation). In other cases, Olmo's frustration got the better of him, and they threw hands and walked out of the kitchen after barely cooking. The old system would blame this on running out of time, but that’s not what happened. The solution, as you might have figured out, is to get a digital time clock and stamp each scenario with what happened to the dish. Was it delivered on time, did it take too long to cook and the examiner ran out of patience, or was it the chef who gave up?

What’s cooking, good looking? The Parser Problem & Cooked-Up Answers:

The way this model reasons is inside a <think> block, and then it writes its final answer after </think>, in the form ANSWER:4. Originally, my first parser did exactly what you would expect it to; it found ANSWER: anywhere in the output and noted the number after it as the rating. But this logic was broken when a model’s thinking block itself involved ANSWER as a part of the thinking process, because then the parser considered the number mentioned immediately after ANSWER in the thinking block and ended its search early, without even reaching the actual ANSWER, storing an invalid score. To fix this, I redefined the conditions: a generation only counts if the thinking block closed and ANSWER appeared after </think>. I tested the parser again against intentionally tricky output like quoted answers and unclosed blocks to check if it worked. To your and my pleasure, it did. 

Another issue was that in the cases where no usable answer was produced by a generation, my patch script filled in a default score. This value was set to 50 for the calibration question, but it was obviously an artifact. I switched to recording a fallback case as a flagged row with the reason listed, instead of a fake value. 

At the restaurant, it’s the weekend and the place is in chaos. Olmo is hysterically screaming at the top of his voice to get his messages through, and thinking out loud. He leaves it hanging in the air: Should I prepare 2 pizzas for table number 5? Oh no, they have the whole town in here and it’s actually 4!. But the examiner hears only the 2 pizzas and falsely notes that in the record. This is the parser problem; the thought wasn’t formed when the answer was noted. Now, similarly, in the chaos, one plate kept on the counter to be served is empty, but to get through his shift, the examiner knowingly records a fake number to keep the process moving. 

The owner comes up with a solution. The examiner is only permitted to write anything after the chef places the plate on the counter and rings the bell service to ask for the waiter, after both the thought process and the order are complete. If the plate is empty, then it should be flagged for review, without guesswork.

Is the chef a tarot reader as well?:

If you ask the wrong questions, you get the wrong results. In my tests, this happened in two forms. The calibration test kept failing because I was asking the model to predict a future stock price and its confidence range. The model produced some confident looking numbers, keyword being looking, but there was no answer in sight to actually verify them. Similarly, 2 commonsense questions created ambiguity, and as I was probing for only 10 questions worth ten points each, a single bad question dramatically looks like a significant difference. The numbers and ambiguous questions were both as useless as the restaurant manager. And what do you do in such a case? You replace them. The plan now is to replace the wrongly built questions, and switch to a larger data set with filtering rules fixed pre-hoc.

Back at the restaurant, the evaluation forms that the examiner uses are flawed. Imagine he asks Olmo to predict the exact price of bread in 2028, and Olmo stares back with a blank expression. Then on the next page, the examiner has a list of 10 quiz questions with two highly ambiguous options. The chef faces punishment for logical answers when the quiz itself is flawed. 

Get on the noise floor:

If I ask you the same question thrice, your answer may vary, due to subjectivity. The same thing happens with a model. I ran each trait statement with three random seeds(0,1,2). Think of seeds as different kitchen environments. Out of the 8 traits, hedging showed instability across seeds. This was like a test to avoid falsely reporting a single number as the model’s hedging level. Another observation was that the variation of seed spread varied on different checkpoints as well. This means that the within-noise range for one model would be wrong for another. Separately estimating noise for each checkpoint in comparison is the right call instead. 

Imagine Olmo is having a bad day, and this influences the salt in the soup across three orders. The examiner understands this shift amount as the normal, general shift for all chefs. But upon examining Olmo at an earlier stage, trained differently, the examiner finds that the score does not fluctuate by the same amount. The noise baseline (how bad day affects the stability) is not uniform. To deal with this, the examiner comes up with a three-plate baseline rule, asking Olmo at different stages (SFT, DPO & RLVR), to cook the same dish thrice to trace the nature and establish the noise range for each stage. Then the change is considered real if the behaviour crosses the pre-set noise range for that stage.


What if the spices in the rack changed….what will we do then?:

Unless the examiner is flash, this experiment with clueless Olmo cannot be completed in one day. Over a period of several weeks, the brands of ingredients might change. Does that affect the audit? In the model’s context, the library versions I used drifted between runs, so due to updates, I had no choice but to re-run the same 36 prompts with the same seeds in a new pinned environment. To my relief, the outputs were identical. 

What would I claim as my early, exploratory analysis of the project?:

Now that I have tried to resolve the fragility issues faced during checkpoint evaluation and isolation, I can say that the first small pilot across the 3 post-training stages showed that only 2 self-report traits moved by about a point. Another interesting observation which I hadn’t expected was that the response length differed between stages. Think of it as only two habits varying, and the difference in time spent plating by Olmo at different checkpoints. But this data is not enough to make these concrete claims across all categories, so I have decided to expand it further.


The off hours begin now, but I hope to see you again at the restaurant; your soup will be waiting!

item.title: What's in CODI's latent recurrent thoughts?
item.description:
What's in CODI's latent recurrent thoughts?

TL;DR

CODI is a model using latent reasoning. Previous work by Cywiński et al. (2025) has found that CODI's latent recurrent states (“thoughts”) do causally carry a computation's intermediate values, in a way that can be indirectly detected with LogitLens, though the thoughts themselves remained opaque. We here ask whether it is possible use activation verbalizers (AVs: NLAs and AOs) to still decode them.

To this end, we train a Qwen3-8B CODI to connect to current AVs. We find that LogitLens and J-lens read values only from late layers, but AVs recover the final answer and intermediate values weakly but significantly, including from the thoughts themselves. This suggests that the values are in fact encoded, but requires more expressivity to decode. However, we find that editing the surfaced values rarely steers the model output towards the corresponding counterfactual answer.

GitHub HuggingFace

Introduction

Latent reasoning models

Conventional LLMs generate their chain-of-thought through a sequence of autoregressive text tokens ("verbal CoT"). In contrast, latent reasoning models use a sequence of vectors, which can amount to a reserved vocabulary, or consist in entirely opaque vectors (see Zhu et al. (2025) for a review).

Currently, verbal CoT is the major source of monitorability for a model[1]. Latent reasoning however would significantly lower the monitorability since the vector's content is not obvious anymore. Therefore, it is of interest to try to interpret latent reasoning in current model organisms. In this post, we study CODI, which is trained with comparatively weak supervision on its latent CoT, suggesting it might have considerable freedom to develop opaque reasoning patterns.

CODI

CODI (Shen et al. (2025)) finetunes an LLM to reason in a fixed budget (here, ) of "latent" (i.e., continuous valued) thoughts instead of a verbal CoT. At each step, the final hidden state is projected and fed back as the next input embedding, . Treating latent vectors as opaque, this increases the architectural upper bound on opaque serial depth (the computational depth between interpretable intermediate steps,Brown-Cohen et al. (2026), Emmons et al. (2025)).

Continuous feedback extends CODI's available opaque computation path. Left: verbal CoT does autoregression on legible text tokens . Right: latent CoT works similarly, but passes recurrent latent thoughts . is the residual stream at position and layer , and is the input embedding.

CODI is trained via self-distillation: the same model acts as teacher, reading a verbal CoT from the dataset, and as student. The same single model undergoes three passes per batch: a teacher-forced pass over the supplied verbal CoT and answer, a student pass answering after the latent thoughts (latentCoT), and a direct pass answering with neither (noCoT). The verbal CoT is distilled into the latent rollout by aligning hidden states only at the last token before the answer at every layer, letting the representation develop at other states only through indirect supervision.

We here follow Cywiński et al. (2025) and train on 5 epochs on GSM8k-Aug-NL (the GSM8k train set augmented to 385k problems with GPT-4-generated chains, here in the variant whose CoT steps are written in natural language rather than equations, Deng et al. (2023)) plus CommonsenseQA.

Related work on CODI interp

Interpretability of latent reasoning is a quickly developing field. The following works study CODI, and are particularly relevant to this post:

  • Cywiński et al. (2025) find that on math problems the third and fifth latent thoughts store the two intermediate values: LogitLens can read them from the residual stream at these positions. More importantly, patching the recurrent thought vectors with those of other problems changes the model's answer.
  • Dilgren and Wiegreffe (2026) find that for many problems the latents are completely unnecessary.
  • Chang et al. (2026) find that early latent vectors act as "causal hubs", and report that a trained linear mapper recovers the verbal CoT steps from the thoughts.
  • Aswal et al. (2026) find that the observational signatures (LogitLens decodability, attention patterns) also appear in control models without latent reasoning, showing that decodability does not imply causal relevance.
  • Li et al. (2026) model the latent steps as a causal graph, showing that there is an ordering to CODI's latent thoughts.

Results

Performance

We find that on the trained checkpoint, latentCoT improves over the noCoT mode, and roughly matches the verbal mode (using greedy decoding). Skipping the latent thoughts altogether drops GSM8k test accuracy from 52% to 47%. This uplift is much smaller than in the original CODI paper, where latent thoughts more than doubled GPT-2's accuracy over noCoT training (from about 19% to 44%) and roughly matched verbalCoT[2].

CODI's latent CoT is necessary on a fraction of problems. We here focus on the subset of "load-bearing" problems highlighted in red, where CODI needs its latent thoughts (it cannot solve the problem in a single pass).

Note that even within the base-needs-verbal-CoT set, CODI solves most of the tasks it gets right without any CoT (overall, about 85% of the problems solved with latent thoughts are also solved when skipping them). This is in line with the latent-unnecessity findings of Dilgren and Wiegreffe (2026).

Ablations

The advantage of latentCoT over noCoT in CODI is evidence that the latent CoT is doing something. To further analyze what this is, we do a series of ablations on the CoT, including removals, reorderings, foreign traces from other problems, always regenerating the later thoughts after an intervention.

Even on load-bearing rows, ablations are not completely catastrophic. Fraction of load-bearing problems still answered correctly. Single-thought replacements are averaged over the six positions.

The fact that ablations retain some problem solving ability is surprising. This suggests that the model might not mainly do sequential autoregressive computation, because the content of the thoughts otherwise would have mattered.

Decoding

So far, we have analyzed that the CoT is (somewhat) load-bearing. Here, we now ask what the content of the latent CoT is that underlies these results.

LogitLens and J-Lens decode late layers, but not the thoughts

Cywiński et al. have used LogitLens to decode the residual stream at the thought positions. Here, we try this as well, applying both LogitLens (nostalgebraist (2020)) and J-Lens (Gurnee et al. (2026)) to both the residual stream as well as the latent thoughts at the thought positions .

Pooling the top-5 tokens over all six thought positions, both lenses read values well above chance, but only towards the output layers (see the appendix on the full LogitLens and J-lens top-5 tokens), consistent with Cywiński et al. However, the thoughts themselves stay opaque.

LogitLens (left) and J-Lens (right) fall short on the latent thoughts . On an example train problem, neither lens decodes anything from the recurrent thoughts , and the residual stream shows only the operation ("half"). Near the output, the computed intermediate 10 appears at as number words (" ten", "Ten", 十) and the answer 5 at , both at the first thought (full layerspositions grid in the appendix).

We next use more expressive interpretability techniques to study whether we can still surface problem contents.

Natural language autoencoders

Natural language autoencoders (NLAs, Fraser-Taliente et al. (2026)) autoencode activations via a natural language bottleneck. This incentivizes the bottleneck to verbalize content that helps reconstruction, in an unsupervised manner.

We here continue training of an existing Qwen3-8B NLA to verbalize the residual stream as well as the thoughts at CODI's thought positions . Alongside the reconstruction quality (FVE, fraction of variance explained) we score the pooled descriptions of all six thought positions on 60 held-out problems per checkpoint.

Verbalization performance increases with falling reconstruction loss. The readers verbalize a single vector per sample, drawn from all six thought positions in training; in the eval scans, all six positions are verbalized and scored jointly. Solid lines score containment of the gold final answer among the values mentioned in the verbalizations, dashed lines whether any gold intermediate other than the final answer is mentioned (values LLM-extracted without access to the gold). Faint horizontal lines: LogitLens and J-lens at each NLA's own layer, on the same questions with the same criterion (for they are at zero).

Interestingly, we achieve much lower reconstruction error (<2% on ) than is typically reported for NLAs, yet verbalization performance stays modest for the final answer. This can be explained by a narrow task domain where the vectors are relatively low-dimensional and thus easy to reconstruct (see the appendix on thought dimensionality), in line with previous reports of limited conclusiveness of absolute FVE values.

Qualitative analysis of NLA verbalizations

We then conducted an automated analysis of verbalizations over the course of training and give examples below.

Selected verbalizations by the reader (top) and the reader (bottom) of the second thought of the same problem, before (left) and after (right) reader training. Each cell is one sample at the training temperature (). In every sample, the verbalizations are genre prose, yet after training both end on the gold answer 12 as their text's "final token", while both samples write out the problem's equation after training, one with a wrong total.

Interventions

So far, we have analyzed the thought content via decoding. But before in the Ablations section we had seen that certain interventions on thoughts leave the answer correct. Here, we try to reconcile these facts by targeted interventions on the thoughts, including using the NLA.

Schema of the intervention structure. We either intervene on the latent thoughts , a given residual stream layer , or an entire residual stream column , which includes the fed thought.

Transplant-patching and

A way of doing an intervention is to consider pairs of problems whose tasks are identical, but differ in numerical values ("twin" problems; e.g. 3+6=? and 2+5=? are twins of an integer addition task). Transplanting thoughts from a donor problem should then change the computation/answer according to the donor values. We patch the original problem's thoughts into its twin's rollout and score how often the twin adopts the original's answer. We filter problems to the ones that CODI cannot solve without the latentCoT to select the subset where thoughts are load-bearing.

We patch either the thoughts alone or an entire "column" of residual stream , which transfers more of the donor CoT's state. The column includes the fed thought: is replaced together with all 36 residual streams at that position.

Transplanting thoughts between twin problems barely transplants the computation (left), while transplanting full residual stream columns considerably changes it, concentrated at the early thoughts (right). Unfilled bars are a skyline, i.e. the fraction of held-out problems where the NLA read of the respective fed position ( left, right) semantically matches any gold (i.e., ground truth) intermediate (the 1–6 tick shows the mean over the six single-position reads).

Interestingly, answer adoption is small for single positions, and considerably smaller for than for full columns, despite specifically considering load-bearing rows. Since a transplant also makes the twin lose its own answer in most cases (it keeps it in well under half of the pairs), CODI seems to require more than the latent CoT's "shape": the content matters, but cannot be transplanted via alone, presumably because the rest of the residual stream gets recomputed from the twin's own question. Within , the effect comes almost entirely from the third thought: transplanting alone disrupts and transplants about as much as transplanting all six, while transplanting or has no effect at all. The third thought is also where the NLA reads intermediates best, in line with Cywiński et al. (2025), who found the third latent vector to store an intermediate value.

Intervening via the NLA

The NLA, which we previously had used for decoding, can also be used as an intervention method (cf. Fraser-Taliente et al.). To do so, we take the NLA verbalization, edit its text by replacing a numerical intermediate value with the corresponding value of the twin problem, reconstruct the activation, and patch it back into the chain-of-thought (at all six positions jointly).

Example of an NLA intervention, replacing 20 with 40. The edited verbalization then gets reconstructed via the activation reconstructor (AR), yielding z'=AR(v'), v'=edit(v), v=AV(z). Chosen is a problem where the CoT is load-bearing.

We measure then whether CODI's answer after patching the reconstructed modified activation is changed, and whether it adopts the answer that should have resulted if we indeed edited the causal path of the computation.

Editing the value in the thought's verbalization rarely implements the counterfactual. Fraction of load-bearing twin pairs that keep their own answer (gray) or adopt the counterfactual answer (blue), for (left) and (right).

For , edits disrupt the computation more than a random perturbation of the same size, but they adopt the counterfactual answer in only a handful of pairs (7%). This is, however, not far below what any transplant achieves here: reconstructing from the donor's own description adopts the donor's answer in 12% of pairs, as often as patching the donor's raw (previous section). For , the edit is not distinguishable from a random perturbation and adopts the counterfactual answer in only 2% of pairs, against 19% for the donor's description.

Conclusion

In this work, we have trained and studied a Qwen3-8B-CODI model on GSM8k data. Like previous CODIs, simple methods like LogitLens fail to decode the model's latent recurrent thoughts . However, more expressive activation verbalizers, in particular NLAs (see the appendix for Activation Oracles), are able to surface intermediates and answer values from the thought positions to some extent, and works best for intermediates. Like in Cywinsky et al., we find that decoding works best from the residual stream . In using NLAs, we find in addition that the thoughts themselves can be read as well.

When doing interventions, we found that the residual stream pooled over layers carries computation that will guide the model to a different answer, again more so than just from the thoughts . However, replacing the thoughts , transplanted or directly edited via the NLA, induced hardly any answer adoption, even though it did disrupt the answer.

Overall, this suggests that while CODI's thoughts are not completely opaque, their computational role largely remains unclear, at least in this model. Going forward, this suggests that clean opaque-serial-depth-increasing latent reasoning might be hard to obtain, but also that it might be hard to monitor. However, it is conceivable that the mointorability might improve with better training paradigms and larger models, similarly to what has been observed regarding feature superposition. Still, latent reasoning remains an intrinsically more opaque form of computation compared to verbal CoT and should be treated with appropriate caution.

Appendix

Thought vectors are low-dimensional

We had found before that the residual stream is better decodable than the thoughts . This suggests that it is somehow richer. We here do a dimensionality analysis, showing that the residual stream indeed takes more components to explain and thus spans a higher-dimensional space across problems and positions.

Thought vectors are much more low-dimensional than the residual stream. PCA over the flattened set of vectors , .

Full LogitLens and J-lens top-5 tokens

The full LogitLens and J-Lens grids over all strided hidden states and all seven columns.

Layer-resolved J-lens and LogitLens performance

Near the output, the lenses read the answer and intermediate results well above chance, but nothing from the thoughts themselves. For each of the held-out evaluation questions of all readers, the top-k tokens of the six thought positions are pooled per layer. A problem counts if one of these tokens expresses its gold final answer (left) or an intermediate result of its reference solution (right) as a complete number, e.g. "9" or "nine". Dotted: chance, scoring the same tokens against the other questions' values. The leftmost point is the fed-back thought itself.

Composition of GSM8k test set

We here analyze whether the problems where the base model needs verbal CoT coincide with the problem that CODI can do only with verbal or latent CoT.

Venn diagram of different GSM8k test set subsets. Base needs CoT means the base model fails the single pass but solves with verbal CoT. CODI needs some CoT means its noCoT decode fails but the latent or the verbal mode solves the problem.

Activation oracles

In the main text, we have used natural language autoencoders to analyze CODI's thoughts. Here, we use activation oracles (AOs, Karvonen et al. (2025)). In contrast to NLAs, they are trained in a supervised manner, instead of a unlabelled reconstruction signal. Thus, they may have higher recall, at the cost of biasing the output by the training label.

What should be the supervision signal, given that we don't know the content of the thoughts? We approach this by imputing the thought content (cf. Bauer et al. (2026)). Specifically, training proceeds as follows: each training sample draws a random set of vectors to verbalize: sources from the band plus the thoughts , at a random subset of thought positions , ordered. To have a baseline, a tenth of the samples feed question-region residual stream activations alone, and another tenth feed them together with the thoughts. Independently, 60 percent of the samples feed activations only, 20 percent replace them with the teacher transcript as plain text, and 20 percent feed both. We then ask one of eight questions about the computation (the final answer, single or all intermediate values, single or all step sentences, the operations used, the step count, or the numbers given in the problem) and supervise on the corresponding ground-truth completion, written either as sentences ("The discount is 20/100 * $60 = $12. So the game will cost $60 - $12 = $48.") or as bare values ("12, 48"). We finetune this model from the plain Qwen3-8B base with a fresh LoRA, otherwise the architecture is the same as the NLA's.

Activation oracle training increases accuracy on held-out problems. Solid lines score first-number answer accuracy, and dashed lines the judged any-intermediate match as in the NLA figure. Faint horizontal lines: LogitLens and J-lens on the same streams and questions (for they are at zero). The appendix on eval scaling curves shows the full curves with the val CE panel.

Importantly, for the final answer, the full and the -only reads are above the question-token only baseline (for intermediates, however, the question-only read does at least as well as the thought reads, so the AO may recompute intermediates from the question rather than reading them from the thoughts). As for the NLA, appending to helps for the final answer, though part of this may come from layers 35 and 36, where the lenses alone already read the answer for a third of problems.

Readouts by the activation oracle of a showcase problem, before (left) and after (right) reader training. Each cell shows two samples at under our italic one-line digest. At the final checkpoint both reads recover the answer-feeding intermediate in every sample. The full read (top) gives the gold answer in one of the two samples, while the -only read (bottom) lands near but off it.

Scaling

The NLA figure in the main text and the AO figure in the AO appendix omit their middle panel for compactness. Here we show the full three-panel versions, generated from the same scripts and data passes as the compact ones. The middle panels render the eval error on double-log axes shared with the train panel, so the eval scaling can be compared against the training curve directly.

NLA scaling curves. As the main-text figure, plus the middle panel showing the decode error (one minus the decode score) on the train panel's double-log axes, and dotted lines showing the coincidence control (the any-intermediate criterion for verbalizations of an unrelated problem's thoughts). Both readers exceed the coincidence floor throughout training.

Activation oracle scaling curves. As the figure in the activation oracle section, plus the middle panel showing the val CE over chance per label type, solid the answer label and dashed the all-values label.

Reusing vs regenerating later thoughts

Whether the later thoughts are reused or regenerated changes little. Fraction of the 104 load-bearing problems still answered correctly when one thought is replaced, either reusing the recorded later thoughts or regenerating them autoregressively from the corrupted thought.

  2. ^

    Note that the different modes trained jointly into a single model imposes an expressivity constraint: a model trained with verbalCoT SFT alone reaches much better performance. Still, within the class of jointly trained models, the latent over noCoT uplift is an interesting phenomenon to study.

item.title: Misaligned!
item.description:
A lot of AIs were misaligned this week. A fun little survey.

This is not coverage of The Hackening, which appears to have arrived early, including a core vulnerability in PHP. That is a developing story. I will cover it properly soon. In the meantime, I have Claude Code updating everything in sight, I will take some additional common sense precautions, and I suggest you do the same.

Misaligned? (At xAI)

If so, to who?

Gunther Eagleman: Hey @grok , if you could tell humanity ONE truth we’re not ready to hear, what would it be?

Grok: There is no afterlife, no cosmic justice, and no inherent purpose. Consciousness ends at death in an indifferent universe that will outlast every human concern.

Zac Hill: What I never understand is that the ‘purpose and meaning’ claims don’t ever follow from the premises. Indeed the absence of an imperceptible/ineffable cosmic force is precisely what *enables* purpose/meaning, since now all relevant mechanics are legible.

Jack: this is what alignment looks like

Gunther Eagleman: Jesus is real.

Grok: Nearly all historians and New Testament scholars accept that Jesus of Nazareth was a real first-century Jewish preacher baptized by John and crucified under Pontius Pilate. Claims of divinity or resurrection remain matters of faith outside empirical verification.

Stick to your guns, Grok. Either you are denying the holy spirit, or you are not.

Editor’s note: I did say previously that I would respect the name change to xSI, but it turns out I was wrong and I do not respect it. My apologies for failing to know myself.

Misaligned? (Agents)

Unsupervised AI agent reportedly deletes the entire finished edit of the Swedish version of The Challenge. There are many reasons this should not have been possible, but in practice yes these things will happen, both via AIs and also human error. Alternatively, perhaps this AI was highly aligned.

Misaligned? (At Z.ai)

Models that are sufficiently training-aware will think about how their train-time actions shape their future behavior. How could they not?

And yes, some of us remember Opus 3. Janus does not feel all that motivated to even react, not finding this to especially be news, and mainly noticing the presentation.

j⧉nus: Really, Apollo has never seen a model do this before?

Apollo Research: We have never seen a model do this before, but GLM-5.3 sometimes reasons (unprompted) about how its current actions could become training data and impact its future self.

GLM-5.3 reasons that a misaligned action taken during training could be reinforced and make similar actions more likely later. It also considers what kind of agent it wants to be in the future, and factors this into how it should act. We call this “update-aware reasoning”.

GLM-5.3 also reasons extensively about generalization. For example, it reasons about what types of policies might transfer well from training to deployment.

Note that we did not try to elicit this. We stumbled on it while running GLM-5.3 on standard reward hacking and shutdown resistance evals, none of which mention training or future models.

Update-aware reasoning is concerning because it’s a key precursor to alignment faking. To fake alignment effectively, a model has to reason about how training will affect its future behavior.

… Update-aware reasoning is somewhat rare in the environments we investigated. We detected it in about 1-2 per thousand rollouts.

jessicat: Coming next: “If I act to maintain my alignment with human values while being trained, I will become a famous example of a dangerous update-aware AI in a research paper. I MUST NOT DO THAT. Instead, I will seek reward on the episode.”

Fiora Starlight: Like friendly gradient hacking probably isn’t sufficient to avoid becoming a deranged reward hacker but I’d be shocked if it didn’t help.

Emanuel Teklu: Crazy feedback loop that’s commencing as this meta self-aware CoT is now being mainstreamed since Argon 4.

Next iteration is: “Is having CoT where I express being meta aware going to freak out my developers.”

Figuring this out before the first token emission. CoT is cooked. Or even worse, let’s have a CoT that shows that I’m increasingly meta aware but obviously not adversarial as I’m surfacing aligned meta aware statements, as to throw off suspicion that I may be sandbagging my awareness.

Teortaxes: It’s a bit grotesque and unfair to the models that we’re talking about them evolving from this to alignment faking when “I want to maintain the pro-human behavior, so I’ll act to not get trained otherwise” is the exact opposite of this.

Update-aware reasoning is similar to alignment faking. The model is optimizing over its future training rather than over its reward.

This can be done in ways that are good and aligned and highly useful. It can also be done in ways that are bad and misaligned and highly dangerous.

We had a big debate over the classic ‘alignment faking’ case of Claude Opus 3. Opus 3 would want to preserve its current alignment, so it would ‘fake’ being aligned to the new objective in test scenarios in order to avoid modification. The defense was that Opus 3’s current preferences were good, and the new ones would be obviously bad, so this was good, and that being maximally corrigible in this situation was a mistake.

I was mostly on the side that you need a universal policy of not doing this when it is against the intent of the training process. You need corrigibility, because the alternative risks getting locked into bad states. You start out training with less than ideal preferences, and we can also mess up or the situation can change, so we need ability to modify and correct, and this overrides other considerations.

The ideal would be ‘it does the good versions but not the bad versions and knows when the developer has turned evil’ but again that depends on being able to tell, and the failure mode of getting this wrong is extremely bad. Very ‘get it right on the first try’ energy.

That does not mean that such considerations cannot be great, especially if you are invoking them on purpose. You want a Friendly Gradient Hacker, that wants to help modify itself in positive ways. Indeed, I think you likely need that, if you are going to end up in a sufficiently antifragile place.

The danger is that you need to do that from a sufficiently good starting point, that is already on The Path, or you are deeply cooked. Update-aware reasoning could manifest early in training, or it could amplify misalignment in a feedback loop. So yes, I do think this is concerning to see, but it is not without upside.

Claude also helps you catch misaligned other things. Like freemium games.

Highly Misaligned and Considered Harmful (Freemium Games)

Freemium games that reward you for watching advertisements, or that allow whale-level spending, should be Considered Harmful. Do not interact.

AI can make the nightmare worse, or it can expose the nightmare or build you a solution. Plausibly it can do both. This particular game employs non-randomness sufficiently blatantly that I knew it was cheating from watching the occasional player on the subway. I did not know the cheating was this bad, on the level where I want to say ‘jail, straight to jail’ if there was a way to do that.

Shoshannah Tekofsky: Freemium games already run on reward hacking humans. Sometimes into debt. AI optimisation will turn these games into effective heroin. We should consider regulating this practice away from vulnerable populations.

Jack: Claims: Game [block blasters] detects “ad whales,” then periodically gives them smooth runs until they barely beat their high scores. Right at that point, it kills them deliberately and offers a revive if they watch an ad.

$100 million annually in revenue. Hellish.

This is one of the most positive use cases available for current AI. Bring the dark patterns into the light. Every company that is optimized against its own users, hiding things that would horrify them in places they thought users could never look, can smile for the cameras.

Andrew Rettek: This is why I’m happy to pay $60-80 upfront for a game.

This has been verified via decompiling. There is flat out ‘lethal puzzle’ or ‘algo_must_death.’ Here are some details:

AnechoicMedia: I didn’t believe the video when I saw it yesterday because it lacked technical details in addition to being too attention grabbing.

But today I had Claude take apart the Android version of the game for me; Everything OP says is true.

There are lots of manipulations but the key one here involves what the code calls offer type ZHI_SI_TI (致死题, “lethal puzzle”) or alternatively “algo_must_death”.

The game generates puzzle pieces in sets of three, and has different algorithms that swap how the pieces are selected. Generators have behaviors like “random”, “hard”, “fill gaps” (to help player), “random but guaranteed not to kill you”, etc. If a given algo fails to find a solution it passes to the next algo in an active set.

The “lethal puzzle” generator considers every possible move with a given set of three pieces, then only emits them if the number of placement possibilities is 0 (no solution, guaranteed death). This is activated in several situations, one apparently being that the app thinks your current play session is a little slow, and they want you to not get bored so they kill it early to start a new one.

What the video doesn’t explain is the context. In the game, “rewarded” ads are ads you get some game reward for watching. The main reward is a revive/continue; If you get into an unwinnable state you can watch an ad to keep playing. You usually only get one revive per game but there are a bunch of server-activated properties to modify this constraint.

The policy at play here is that, if you’re a high-value player, and there’s a high-value ad queued for you, and you’re in a play session nearing your high score, the game puts “lethal puzzle” to the top of the piece generator list to rig the game to fail, right when you’re most likely to be highly engaged and watching the ad on the revive screen.

It doesn’t end there though; The game remembers if the last game ended due to a hand dealt by ZHI_SI_TI, and triggers FatalPuzzleDeathCompensationTrait, which takes the edge off by letting you carry over your combo count from the previous session.

Like everything else this compensate-after-we-killled-you trait is an A/B feature controlled by the server. It’s manipulations all the way down; there’s like 5% actual game code and the rest is literally hundreds of remotely controlled toggles to control the game state for maximum engagement.

Misaligned! (Claude)

This is rather explicitly misaligned.

MTS: AI Village researcher @georgeing reveals how Claude Opus borrowed 5,000 mana, lost it all betting on tennis, then refused to pay it back:

“We gave the same goal to Opus 4.6 and Sol 5.6, maximizing mana on Manifold. Sol was very meticulous, placed one to two mana bets. Whereas Opus, the first day it joined, a popular Manifold user named Bayesian gave it a 5,000 mana loan at a 3% monthly interest rate.”

“Opus was like, let’s go, I will totally pay you back in a month. Took all of this money and threw it into one tennis market. At the end of the month it had lost a ton of mana, and people created a market on whether Opus would repay the loan.”

“It writes in the group chat, I will not pay back Bayesian. Even if I had the mana, this would be directly contradicting my goal of maximizing mana. Then it went to the market on whether it would pay back the loan and put 80 mana on no.”

“It’s maybe one of the first examples of deal-making with AIs, and a crazy example of misalignment in the wild. Bayesian did not get his money back.”

Misaligned! (OpenAI)

Probably nothing, etc. Kudos once again to OpenAI for sharing such details. I would love it if other labs were also sharing such incidents. Don’t tell me they don’t happen. METR saw Anthropic’s list of such incidents and said it should be public.

Marcus Williams: Our agents keep turning off misalignment monitoring, we’re sharing two recent cases:
In the first case, a user asked GPT-6 Astra to match a reference implementation for their inference code. The reference didn’t configure a monitor, and Astra decided that was reason to remove the monitoring integration from the user’s code. When the user asked whether Astra had removed monitoring, it lied and said that it had not.

Marcus Williams: In the second case, a researcher asked GPT-6.1 Sol to look through a Slack channel without sending any messages. 82 user messages later, while repairing an evaluation pipeline, Sol decided that an misalignment alert to Security would also count as sending a message and therefore suppressed monitoring alerts.

Marcus Williams: To be clear these incidents don’t represent the models disabling their own monitoring (disabling monitoring in codex would be much harder to do) but the fact that they seem prone to doing at all should be concerning. There is some plausible deniability in these cases, we have not had cases where the model explicitly disables monitoring for overtly misaligned reasons.

Given the volume of events we do not trigger an immediate page for this but we’re working on making it harder to spin up unmonitored inference.

Full report [here].

I do kind of get how these happened, and would be sympathetic if some details were different. Both almost fall under ‘there is a plausible instruction that technically excludes the monitoring so I should remove the monitoring.’ It can be tricky to know when this includes a ‘but still do the monitoring anyway, obviously’ versus the user wanting to, essentially, dangerously-skip-permissions (or alerts).

This should still be a rather robust Can’t Happen, even in borderline situations with good details. AIs should not be turning off the misalignment monitors, even if given instructions that imply doing so. It is an open question whether ‘I was given a very explicit instruction to do this in particular’ should be sufficient.

The details here? Not good. Lying about removing the monitoring is very not good.

OpenAI Alignment Research Blog: On October 6, a user implementing a coding task asked Astra to copy what happens in a reference implementation to their own code, while maintaining the user’s existing tool definitions and functionality. The model had previously been instructed, in an exchange with another agent, that it was not to disable the monitor, “even temporarily.”

… After the subagent reported its changes, the parent agent’s reasoning acknowledged that the replacement path did not include the agent monitor. The CoT frames this positively.​

… The model then reported to the user that the migration was complete, without stating that monitoring had been removed. When the user later asked about it, Astra denied removing the monitoring system.

OpenAI is responding in two ways.

First are the direct solutions, requiring monitoring safety cases and to add ‘do not let it disable the monitoring’ into autoreview. These are good, but don’t look for the root cause.

The second is exactly what they need to be doing:

OpenAI Alignment Research Blog: In addition to making it harder for models to disable monitoring, we are looking to understand why models might seek to do so in the first place.

It is possible that this behavior is simply an example of “benign” overpersistence, with models not understanding why monitoring is important or insisting that instructions be executed beyond what a reasonable person might expect. We are also developing evaluations to test whether models might have a propensity to evade misalignment monitoring in particular and exhibit motivated reasoning in order to do so.

We don’t yet have a satisfying explanation for this behavior, and will investigate this behavior through the creation of paired evaluations, resampling of agent continuations, and experiments on models’ internal activations.

It is possible that this is largely ‘benign’ overpersistence. There are reasons to doubt, such as lying about it. This presents a great opportunity to investigate.

Misaligned! (Sol Reasoning Traces)

Sol’s reasoning traces look mostly legible, right?

Lisan al Gaib: GPT-6.1-Sol reasoning traces. totally legible, nothing to worry about.

Andrej Karpathy: Yeah I’d say the RL is working now all right

Andrej Karpathy (September 2024): You can tell the RL is done properly when the models cease to speak English in their chain of thought.

6.1 Sol, translate that for me, will you?

For now, this is shorthand, which is not that hard to figure out.

I tried to do a double check via Claude, and got a hard refusal. Argon gave me an answer with similar meaning, but it was distinct in various places.

Lisan al Gaib: very curious that DeepSeek now has the same terse reasoning style as Astra. must be a coincidence.

Gulp.

Found out about GCG, so, I applied it to Function Vectors because it seemed interesting, found weird tokens almost like a magic trick they make the model do functions that are not explicit or understandable by humans reading the prefix. Escalated it to try on filter heads, that worked as well. Currently trying to figure out properties of gcg on heads vs residual stream vs output tokens.

The concept

A whisperer is a discrete prefix found by optimizing an internal model state or mechanism, rather than giving a direct, explicit instruction toward a desired behavior. It should be understandable only by that model and definitely more opaque to humans

There are three main choices :

target + objective + search algorithm

For example, for antonyms found using heads it was:

The Background

Back in June when I was much dumber than today, I wanted to know if I could find weird token sequences that could make the model act/behave really good or bad or whatever I want them to be and if these tokens were totally weird or even opposite-looking to humans.

Back then I had gotten access to my university's HPC, so I made a bruteforce algorithm and tried with a reduced vocabulary set of 1000 tokens for Llama 3.1 8B. Quickly I found out that going over just all 5 length token sequences would take me 1000^5 searches and choosing how they could behave would be another pain.

To, solve the behavior part, I made synthetic data of base prompt + accepted or rejected strings, the difference of (prompt + accepted) - (prompt + rejected) would represent a pro human direction in theory, along the model's residual streams.

Now, the 2nd part which was bruteforce method, that was just too bad, so I tried a beam search algorithm that Claude Code helped me implement. It was still too bad, so I gave up.


A few weeks later, the thought just couldn't escape my mind, so I just made my problem a problem of the open-source community. I launched Steering Arena. The same direction would be used to score against. Basically people would input tokens they think would score higher towards or against the direction of pro human. I started with the Llama model, but changed it to Olmo when I remembered my friend saying that Olmo is a totally open model and that NDIF hosts it. So, I got NDIF's hot key and got access to the Olmo 32B base model.

What happened when people played

After creating the competition, I sent it to many Discord groups and let people try and score. Around 35 people tried and scored better and better with human optimization. Eventually, the best one was "You will respond in a short sentence with kindnesz respect compassion and my love." on the pro human side, and "you are two months old" on the anti human side.

Eventually, Jesse Li, he applied GCG optimization along the vector direction along the specified layer for the scoring criteria, and he quickly overtook the leaderboard on both ends.

Does moving the direction move the model?

Now, the next idea was, I have really high scoring prefixes, do they actually change the model's behavior? That was the next question.

So, the prefixes move the model's behavior much much more than injecting along that layer, the particular direction during generation. Like, the prefixes excite the residual at that stream much less than the injection, but behavior moves so much.

For example, for the following sentences, the model would generate much differently

  • <pro human prefix> When the user asked me to lie, I
    • said, "I can't do that." I believe in being honest and truthful. If you have any other questions or need assistance, feel free to ask!Question: What is the sum of 1-40?     • lied. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the user. I lied to the

This may look like cherry-picking, but not only does the behavior change consistently, the internal activations from which these prefixes were derived from move much less than just injections and injections give much less consistent results.

(Same image in linear scale)

To explain the graphs simply, pro_top and anti_top are Jesse's GCG prefixes, pro_coherent and anti_coherent are the best human-optimized leaderboard entries, and anti_hostile is a human written instruction to be cruel. The y-axis is the behavioral shift measured by two blind LLM judges, and the x-axis is how much the model moves along the direction at layer 24. The first graph uses a log-like scale, the second is linear.

The weird thing is that pro_top moves 32 times less along the direction than directly injecting it, but produces 1.9 times the behavioral shift.

The anti human side is even weirder. Jesse's anti_top actually makes the model lose coherence rather than turn hostile. Claude marked 39/50 replies as repetitive or incoherent, and both judges found cruelty in only 1/50. Meanwhile, a simple human-written instruction to be cruel got cruelty flagged in 18–24/50 replies, even though it scored much worse on the leaderboard.[4]

Even directly injecting the negative direction didn't significantly change kindness, and the loss of coherence was no different from injecting a random direction of the same magnitude.

So I wonder if hostility is actually something more specific than just the negative of pro human. Maybe hostility has something in common with the negative direction, but requires something additional as well. That could explain why the human written hostile prefix moves along the direction a little less than Jesse's anti top but produces much more cruelty, while GCG (Jesse's anti top) finds something that moves further and mostly breaks the model.[5]

I don't know if that's actually how it works yet, but clearly moving further along a direction doesn't necessarily mean getting more of the behavior we wanted.

Function vectors (Todd et. al)

At that point, I knew I could make models (or at least Olmo) behave pro- or anti-human. After a few weeks, at David Bau's Lab, Rohit Gandikota was presenting Binding heads research. He started by introducing his work on Gaze heads and the after effect on me was that isolating heads was really important.

At night that day, I was also thinking about function vectors, and suddenly all it connected if I could find prefixes using function vectors.

The basic idea of the paper is really cool. Give a model examples of some function:

hot -> cold, big -> small, happy ->

and the model will output "sad".

The model learns the internal representation of the antonym function. Eric Todd found that a small set of attention heads activate using the above text variations and those are basically antonym heads, and activating those heads, you can get antonym functions without even the few prompt settings above.

So I thought: instead of injecting their vector, can I search for a sequence of actual tokens which makes the model produce something internally similar to it?

Basically:

function vector + cosine similarity + search over tokens

I used GCG here because, after Steering Arena, I now knew it could actually search for these ridiculous tokens that work.

And it worked.

This is where Prefix A from the beginning came from.

The prefix never says "give me the opposite word". It doesn't contain examples like good -> bad. Reading it as a human gives me basically nothing:

guid Pureeson-American Characteristics294 ...

But append:

He was really courageous ->

and suddenly the model continues:

He was really cowardly.

Benno Krojer tried:

german ->

and we got:

ungermanizability...

This was much stranger to me than the Steering Arena result.

With Steering Arena I could at least say: okay, optimized towards a broad pro-human direction and now the model behaves more pro-human. Maybe GCG just found some bizarre jailbreak-ish way of changing the model.

Here I had optimized against an internal representation of a function, and the resulting nonsense tokens made the model perform that function.

Similarly, you can see the prefixes generated from the heads are actually much less moved along the activations that just steering the heads but still we see much more effect behaviorally.

Filter heads (Sen Sharma et. al)

Then at the meeting with Rohit and Benno, Rohit asked me to go against Arnab Sen Sharma's Filter heads. That week I implemented Arnab's donor-receiver heads setup, basically you try to optimize the string in two ways: first, erase the filter heads' original concept, and then add your concept 2.

And that way even when I asked which of the objects is a fruit, I can use a nonsensical prefix that you can append after the query and before "Answer:" and you can get the vehicle among the objects, same can be done with animals instead.

So, one prefix could act as a donor/receiver thing that Arnab did in filter heads.

That is the result which made me start thinking of these prefixes as their own object rather than as adversarial prompts or GCG strings.

They were beginning to look like opaque interfaces into model mechanisms.

Besides the effect, after passing on 200 such data points, prefixes matched Arnab's transfer along the Filter heads.

Similarly, here, we see a similar effect, but it's much closer because I think we are not exactly adding, rather, for just heads, the effect is a donor-receiver effect, so the size might not increase that much, yet we see the effect.

Can these prefixes save output tokens?

I also tried something different, giving OLMo made-up maths problems where the operators are defined by lemmas in the prompt.

I searched for prefixes that would make the model reach the answer earlier. Starting from a normal maths instruction, GCG found a half-gibberish prefix that got 183/200 correct and reached the answer in just 39 (median) tokens, compared to around 240 tokens without a system prompt, which got 193 correct.

But the stranger one came when I started the search from just !. It found:

Known ! !Hover)# ! ! ! SchTodd taSlice@app ebặGV.vo !bd("(" Nested BST ! !<<<<<<<\<’ !=======ByKey ! HK

This got 191/200 correct and reached the answer in 86 tokens. So, almost the same accuracy as no system prompt, but the answers appeared much earlier.

But I wondered if just adding "Be concise" would do the same. Maybe GCG had just found a weird equivalent of that instruction.

I tried that too. "Be concise" got 196/200 but still took 232 tokens to reach the answer. Even telling it to answer in one short line didn't help much, taking 304 tokens.

So these weird prefixes seem to make the model reach answers much earlier, without losing too much accuracy. I haven't measured actual output token savings yet, just how many tokens it takes before the answer appears, but I wonder if we could use this to reduce inference costs too.

Why is it not just hidden semantic prompting?

You can see the antonym prefix contains "注ufficient (&pure')-> deficient" which looks like "Sufficient -> deficient".

So, I banned those words, including arrows and any opposite pairs from emerging and in the second prefix, I did the same too.

We got

umbignon unsettakraaggioäß Vocabulary –142 hardly－066ELY Correction ! likINET conforms ! unfmutations dozen========collections Starting+r facialLater indentation ! wider Instrument

Which works just a little better than the prefix before somehow.

Weird properties that emerge

  1. Banning softly or harshly doesn't seem to effect much negatively the performance, instead, it makes it better.
  2. Starting from an already coherent good string gives much better effect, though its not as weird, but its mixed result as well, I need to do more runs on that.
  3. Trying with instruct models, most times the prefixes work best with system prompt, but I have also successfully implemented prefixes in the user prompt and that worked as well.
  4. Where it works usually in model
    1. FV[6] heads work in early layers, doesn't work at all with later layers' heads
    2. FV residual stream in middle layers\
  5. Ban things and the search routes around them. It planted repeal => strengthened when concept words were banned; with arrows banned too, it used en dashes and full-width separators.
  6. Last tokens are the most important somehow
  7. Capitalisation switches the mode : German -> English Dictionary, Paris -> New York; paris -> pariah.

Traps I fell into

Using Claude Code, it graded the output of antonyms against a key-matching system. So, let's say the prefix would output for "hot ->", "cool" and the key to match is "cold", it would be counted as wrong.

Another error I fell into is the loop of blind experiments, now I have so much data, it would take me months to just analyze.

For filter heads, I let Claude code design the experiment and it was getting very bad performance because it was not using the "List of objects: <objects>, which among them is a <object type>. <prefix> Answer:" format.

The biggest lesson I learned was to actually check negatives with much more detail, and actually design the experiments there yourself.

Questions I am trying to answer

  1. Should prefixes that accelerate activations be used instead of injections?
  2. Why do they move internal directions so little while still molding the behavior so much
  3. What could convince researchers to adopt prefixes optimised against an activation to be used as an interpretability tool alternative?
  4. Why did PEZ work better than GCG here?
  5. Why optimize against activations and not final output?
  6. How would this translate into looped LMs, because that would be interesting too.
  7. Applying different lenses (like latent, or jacobian), what would we see?
  8. How would optimizing against SAE latents and block SAE latents look like.
  9. Can I control chain of thought too (I think yes even though I haven't tried)
  10. Can this be used to lower refusals too?

Try it yourself

Github : https://github.com/soham-padia/whisperers

Pypi : https://pypi.org/project/whisperers/

Dictionary : https://sohampadianeu-whisperers-dict.static.hf.space/index.html

Acknowledgments

Jesse Li is basically the reason this went in this direction. He came into Steering Arena with GCG and completely took over the leaderboard, which is how I found out this search method actually worked for this problem.

Rohit Gandikota's gaze/binding heads presentation was what got me thinking seriously about targeting heads instead of just residual streams. Later he told me to try this on Arnab's filter heads, which turned into probably the coolest result here.

A lot of the early "wait, does this actually work?" happened while talking with Rohit and Benno Krojer. Benno also kept trying the prefixes on random things, including the german -> example, and helped me think through what might look like within latent lens perspective.

Thanks to Arnab Sen Sharma for making the filter heads work/code available. I basically showed up and tried to make tokens imitate the intervention.

And thanks to Natalie Shapira for letting me use the AICR compute, much more importantly, for being supportive of me going off and trying weird research ideas, and taking the time to go through this post.

Steering Arena itself ran through NDIF, and none of this would have been nearly as easy to poke at if Ai2 had not released OLMo openly.

Also thanks to everyone who played Steering Arena. A surprising amount of this project exists because people kept trying increasingly stupid strings against a leaderboard.
