item.title: D̶o̶n̶’̶t̵⠀Can’t Look Up
item.description:
Why AI development won’t stop and what can realistically be done about it.

If war is so terrible, why do we still actively wage it? If nuclear weapons are so powerful and dangerous that we even came up with the concept of Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD) as a consequence of using them, why do we still keep stockpiles of them? If climate change is a scientifically proven fact whose consequences are not only awful, but global-reaching, why haven’t we successfully addressed it yet? If hunger could have already been eradicated, why haven’t we done so? If many of the most renowned AI scientists have warned against AI’s reckless development, why don’t we pause its development until at least we feel more certain about how to do it safely?

These questions are complex and difficult to address in the world we live in. Or in other words: if these problems were easy to manage, they would already have been solved.

In this post, I am making the claim that two fundamental challenges stand in the way of global coordination: 1) the visibility problem, concerning our ability to understand and agree on the nature and consequences of a threat; and 2) the structural problem, concerning the incentives that drive states to act even against the collective interests of individuals.

It seems to me that most of the current discussion around AI global coordination is missing out on either or both of these problems. Moreover, addressing either in isolation won't be sufficient.

Understanding these two problems helps explain why simply calling for an AI pause is unlikely to succeed—and what a more realistic path toward global coordination might look like. The result is a highly pragmatic (and speculative too, to be fair) take on why we can’t just pause AI development due to the visibility and structural issues and a proposal of the kind of solutions I think are necessary in order to even have a chance at global coordination of the sort needed.

The visibility problem

All states affected by a global challenge need to recognize it as both real and global. They also need to see themselves as sufficiently responsible for addressing it to take action. If they are expected to contribute equally, they will probably also need to perceive the challenge as similarly serious. Otherwise, they will not feel compelled to make comparable contributions.

The structural problem

States operate within an anarchic international order. There is no authority above states that can enforce laws and treaties, even when mutually interested states have signed them. Moreover, states ultimately pursue their own survival. They may care about the well-being of neighboring states, or even all states, but their primary responsibility lies within their own borders, and their survival comes first. States must also contend with substantial uncertainty about other states’ intentions. This uncertainty is a complex product of anarchy, states’ ability to wage war, their pursuit of survival, and other factors. Nonetheless, states cooperate and compete in this environment, both economically and militarily. They recognize that survival is best secured by being strong relative to their competitors. This is Realism 101. Within international relations scholarship, there is plenty of nuance and disagreement, for example about how much domestic affairs and international institutions affect states’ behavior. Without going too deeply into theory, however, anarchy, the pursuit of survival, and uncertainty create structural conditions that affect states’ decisions.

When confronted with a global issue, a state must evaluate possible outcomes through both its own perception of the problem and the structural constraints it faces. In academia, this is perhaps best captured by the security dilemma: one state’s decision to arm itself may look like preparation for aggression to its neighbor, even if its intentions are defensive. The neighbor is then motivated to arm itself in response. This creates a competitive spiral in which neither state may seek confrontation, yet both act according to the structure of the international order. The issue extends beyond military power and appears in many kinds of cooperative initiatives. Cooperation on a particular issue is always assessed through a game-theoretic lens: “What do I gain or lose relative to my competitors?” This occurs in many, if not all, areas of international relations, from climate cooperation to support for political movements, and from international aid to aggression.

The two problems together

Think of the structural problem as the rules of the game and the visibility problem as the players’ ability to see what lies ahead.

AI governance is possibly one of the most consequential global challenges we have ever faced. But before turning to it, let’s briefly consider two other examples.

Climate change

Climate change has posed an important visibility challenge. What would the consequences of inaction be? A decision-maker cannot answer only in general terms: how exactly would inaction affect their state in the years to come? Will it rain more, and by how much? What about heat waves? What consequences should they expect? What specific action would reduce a particular risk by a given amount? How much money should they allocate, and to what or whom? These are real questions that decision-makers have faced when deciding how to respond to climate change, and they are difficult to answer. Climate change illustrates the visibility problem: its effects unfold over years and decades, affect different parts of the world unequally, and involve consequences that are not clearly defined or agreed upon.

From a structural perspective, the problem becomes even muddier. Should all states contribute equally when responsibility for the problem is so unevenly distributed? If the consequences affect some states more than others, what ensures that less affected states also cooperate, or contribute as much? If reducing my state’s CO₂ emissions means slowing the development that earlier industrialized states benefited from, why should I now have to slow my own progress? How will climate cooperation affect my position relative to competitors in the years to come? Will I be better or worse off?

Those questions have structural reasons behind them and even if states see the challenge as real, they may still strategically “defect” as they see the benefits of doing so, relative to other players, as greater.

Nuclear weapons proliferation

A very different example is nuclear weapons. From a state’s decision-making perspective, nuclear weapons differ fundamentally from climate change: their visibility is crystal clear. Their capabilities and consequences were made vivid by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki and by the many nuclear tests that followed. Through this clarity, nuclear weapons became the most effective deterrent. It became clear what the consequences of attacking a nuclear-armed state would be.

This visibility also created a powerful structural incentive for other states to pursue nuclear weapons. The security dilemma associated with nuclear proliferation was particularly vivid during the Cold War. Once the United States had nuclear weapons, the Soviet Union felt threatened and pressured to develop its own. Once both had them, each felt it needed more weapons to ensure that it could retaliate with equal or greater force if attacked. This led to a cycle of nuclear armament in which the destruction of the other side could be assured, giving rise to the concept of mutually assured destruction.

The reason the nuclear standoff never escalated into war, despite its close calls, was that all parties could clearly see the consequences. Unlike climate change, nuclear proliferation was “blessed” with immense visibility for the states involved. Had the consequences been less clear, nuclear weapons would likely have been used. I have simplified the history considerably for the sake of argument, but broadly speaking, this is the main reason nuclear weapons have not been used again in war.

AI governance

In his September 2026 post We Must Pace the Frontier, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei proposes slowing AI development through coordination among democracies whilst widening their lead over China. He argues that “these measures increase the leverage held by democracies and make an agreement more likely in the future.” Unfortunately, I think this assessment is overly optimistic. Those same measures could strengthen China’s incentives to accelerate its own development and resist an agreement intended to preserve its competitors’ advantage. I see similar limitations in many proposals from frontier AI lab CEOs, academics, and think tanks. Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares do a good job of explaining the likely outcome of developing advanced AI, yet they do not propose a structurally compatible solution.

I will explain this using the two foundations laid out earlier: the visibility problem surrounding AI governance and the structural constraints affecting states’ decisions.

The visibility problem surrounding AI

First, let me approach the problem from an uncommon angle.

One of the first things people notice about AI is how much it resembles science fiction. Its potential, its lack of precedent, and the speed of its development all contribute to this impression. I want to begin by examining AI’s visibility problem from a communication perspective.

The way language works, in a nutshell, is that you (the emitter) trust someone (the receiver) to have the same knowledge as you do (or close enough) of a certain word and combination of words, when you use them, therefore expecting him to receive the same message as you formulate it in your mind (or as close as possible given your ability to put it into words).

However, language is far from precise. Describing subjective things like emotions or feelings is terribly hard because of the very fact that it is subjective. The words "terrible" and "beautiful" are very imprecise because there is no clear objective way to correlate the word with a real-world "object" as that correlation requires both context and perception.

Similarly, when we are to describe things we have not seen or experienced before, we often “lack words” to describe them. Or we use the wrong words for it. This is, one, because if the "object" to describe has never happened before, then there is no precedent for describing it, and, two, because we are likely to not even understand what the object is, how it came to be or what its purpose is, or other "metadata" that would help us define it.

This is exactly what is happening now with AI. I mean, the very word "AI" is used for very different undefined things. When used to refer to AI as a "whole"—as the industry or as the sum of all models, or the top models—it assumes the receiver understands it as well as you do, which is btw a massive assumption given the novelty, scale and pace of development. Sometimes AI is used anthropomorphically, describing it as if it has drives or agency the way we understand humans do. Some other times it is used to describe capabilities or outcomes in a way that assumes both the emitter and receiver know what they are talking about, often casually jumping into the shoes of the most cutting-edge experts working on AI research. Words such as “think,” “drive,” and “feel” carry associations with humans, living things, agency, or consciousness.

Do you even realize how shocking this is to most? Casually applying concepts tied to humans, or perhaps other living things, to "machines" is a huge leap. So huge, it even creates a disconnection for the receiver. Like a massive "WTF is he even talking about?" It is not only the fact that we have never had "machines plotting before"; it is that the closest thing we have to it is basically Science Fiction, and a much more far-fetched version of it than flying cars btw. So not only do we not have precedents; it is that the closest related thoughts come entirely from imagination and fiction. Linguistically speaking, this makes effective communication using these terms very hard, to put it mildly.

The same happens with artificial general intelligence (AGI) or artificial superintelligence (ASI). We do not have a clear definition of either, as the very definition often used is vague and non-verifiable (at least not until we are very far beyond the invisible/undefined threshold). Let's take AGI as AI being more intelligent than all the experts in all fields. What does "that" even look like? What even is "it"? It is no wonder that we keep moving the bar by which we would have previously assessed "this is AGI". This is not to say that "AGI" doesn't exist; it is to say we do not know what exactly it even is or means to begin with. The concept is distant from familiar examples, both in its lack of precedent and in its possible effects.

Think of all the terms we use to describe AI and how they are hardly fitting. To say that AI "thinks" would require an accurate description of what thinking for an AI means versus how we understand we think. In fact, it is even more mind-bending than that. Because, to some degree, they seem to think. They seem to feel. At the end of the day, this is what I think of you too. It is only through repetition that I come to assume you are not a simulated NPC but, more likely, someone more closely resembling myself. So where is the threshold, if there is even one, between knowing that you think and knowing that an AI thinks? What’s going to happen when I see a robot that is physically indistinguishable from a human, at least by sight, and acts and talks like a human? So the reason these terms are mind-bending when used around AI is that they are both far (seems SciFi) and so not far (seems more real than yesterday) at the same time.

We use language to the best of our ability. The reason why we sometimes feel "wow, he's such a good speaker or writer" is because we marvel at how others have a much better ability to put into words complex topics than we do. This implies that even though we all use language, we do not use it equally well. Approximation and imprecision are everywhere. Much more so when we do not even know what we are talking about!

The same goes for predictions and percentages of likelihood. A 10% chance of human extinction. Giving it a number like that makes it feel more objective than it really is and at the same time, it comes with its own issues. Assuming we had a crystal ball that would accurately forecast chances of future outcomes, what would be the percentage of human extinction that would warrant action? Moreover, what percentage would warrant what action? Would 5% warrant waging war against states who think 5% is too low and that we should only stop AI development when reaching 15%? Understandably, that % is used to describe the fact that it can happen, but really, the problem is not merely that it can happen; the problem is emotionally reconciling ourselves to the possibility regardless of the percentage.

And one clarification. Even if we could describe "extinction", or death, or consciousness or other difficult terms, it doesn't mean we have an internal model of them; it doesn't mean we "understand" them. Take "a mother losing her son"; we can understand the linguistic meaning of the phrase and intuitively grasp the feelings associated, but we can't understand what it really is unless we have lived through it. We are driven by emotions and feelings, not by reasoning or deterministic goals. This is why stories work well for us btw, because they help build perspective and context around a concept, helping us evoke the same feelings (or close) the emitter wanted to convey much more efficiently than otherwise.

And then comes the harder part. Talking about things when we don't know what we are talking about, in order to do something about them and/or to forecast associated outcomes. I am not even joking. From AI extinction risks to loss of jobs, curing all diseases and extending life, among other wild scenarios. WTF does extinction even mean? We can't even understand what our individual personal death “means”, much less the death of the rest of humans, much less the impossibility of more humans to come after us. The same goes for all the other extreme predictions, whether good or bad. We have a very hard time reconciling ourselves to these concepts because they are so far into imagination land. I mean, when a close relative, someone who we love dearly, passes away, we tend to not believe it or to deny it. It is very hard to swallow that someone who was so dear to us would be gone. It is so hard that it takes painfully living through it to understand it. Try to explain to someone what it feels like. Then take that difficult task and multiply it by n. Or look at it from a very illustrative angle: a news headline stating "Many leading AI labs and AI safety researchers assign a substantial probability, perhaps 5–20%, to AI-driven extinction". Then the next news piece talks about politics or some other irrelevant topic. We are so utterly disconnected from the meaning of such things that we normalize them down to absurdity and ridiculousness.

For published survey results behind this kind of discussion, see Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI, which reports responses from 2,778 AI researchers.

This is why humility about AI’s meaning and consequences is imperative. We try to educate one another about concepts that are difficult to internalize, even for those making the arguments. AI’s visibility challenge is immense, and it calls for epistemic humility.

The structural constraints affecting AI

As with climate change, the difficulty of understanding AI’s consequences affects how states are likely to respond. Following others, I would describe AI as a hyperobject. However difficult it is to understand, states cannot afford to dismiss it. They must weigh its potential against their goals: survival and the subsidiary goals that follow from it, such as the pursuit of power.

Much has been said about this, but let me highlight the features most relevant to states’ interests.

  • No apparent ceiling. AI’s potential is enormous, as demonstrated by its current capabilities, the continued advance of the frontier, the capital invested, and the rapid—possibly exponential—pace of improvement. Its potential is increasingly tied to our imagination about how to use it, rather than to capabilities alone.
  • Extreme dual use. AI could be economically disruptive, to put it mildly, as well as militarily disruptive. Its dual-use potential extends beyond that of previous technologies.
  • Rapid development. The rate of development will make governments fear a narrowing window of opportunity, if it has not already done so. What if progress becomes so rapid that we cross critical thresholds before realizing that we have crossed them?
  • Democratization. Wider access to AI may be a double-edged sword. What if highly capable systems have their weights leaked or released and are then used by small groups for harmful purposes? This concern becomes more relevant as open-weight models become more capable and frontier models demonstrate the ability to conduct cyberattacks, discover zero-day vulnerabilities, and chain vulnerabilities to achieve a goal. Compute is not cheap, but it may become feasible for a small actor to attain a system costing, say, $5–10 million and then run enough agents using unrestricted open-weight models to disrupt critical infrastructure through a cyberattack, or cause something worse.
  • Potential loss of control. AI development is difficult to predict, and the systems themselves can be opaque. We train them through gradient descent over vast numbers of parameters whose interactions no human fully understands. What if we lose control? This possibility is increasingly accepted among leading experts and should be treated as a real scenario. Many of you are already familiar with it, so I will not repeat the case here.
  • The one-shot problem. Given the characteristics above, what if we truly have only one opportunity to get this right? What if failure at a critical step leaves no opportunity to try again? Whether through loss of control, misuse of advanced AI, or dangers we do not yet foresee, if the consequences can be so severe as to cause widespread societal disruption or even extinction, then we only get one chance. This is the one-shot problem and it resembles the black ball analogy Bostrom explained in his Vulnerable World Hypothesis paper.

All these features are subject to the visibility problem. Nonetheless, states consider, and must consider, them to varying degrees because together they present a potential threat to national security.

If these properties of AI are real, and they seem more plausible with each passing day, states will face structural pressures to act in particular ways.

Eventually, a state will be AGI-pilled enough to realize that just as they themselves are envisioning new uses and possibilities of this technology, so are their competitors. Then, the question will arise: will my competitor achieve a first-strike capability or will I, and what happens then? Nuclear deterrence is beginning to weaken due to the apparently unlimited power-creep nature of AI opening new attack vectors. Eventually, if we are not there already, we will find ourselves in a Cold War 2.0 that will grow more dangerous as AI keeps growing more capable. New capabilities, time compression, autonomous actions, etc.

As states consider these scenarios, they will feel pressure to advance because they cannot allow competitors to become stronger. If a state develops a substantially more powerful AI than its competitors and retains control over it, it will be in a position to impose its will, perhaps even achieve global hegemony or prevent others from ever catching up. This creates incentives to advance despite perceived risks. The economic and military incentives are so immense that slowing or stopping development is not feasible.

One might argue that states should negotiate agreements about what to develop and what to pause. But why have states pursued secret nuclear programs? They had incentives to evade constraints, and in some cases, such as North Korea, acquiring nuclear weapons paid off. If the incentives surrounding AI are even greater, why assume that states will not evade an agreement? A more likely scenario is that they seek ways around treaties to keep advancing AI development, driven by the security dilemma. If the United States suspects that China is secretly developing a highly capable AI, it will either seek to stop the program by whatever means are available or pursue its own program to get there first. The same applies in reverse.

Anyone who believes that mutual restraint is the likely outcome is, I’m afraid, moralistically biased and underestimates the gap between group “emergent” behavior and that of individuals. Period. The uncertainty surrounding AI, its capabilities, and its potential is so immense that states have only two credible options: permanently prevent others from developing it further, even through force, or develop it first.

Unfortunately, the current trajectory may lead to a loss of control over AI. Before that, however, we will likely see conflict between great powers, and if that happens, we may no longer have to worry about AI.

A narrow path

Is there a realistic path compatible with both the visibility problem and the structural constraints of the international system?

I want to believe there is.

Bostrom argues that, if the hypothesis (VWH paper) is true and global governance is impossible, then a possible solution to humanity’s survival is through a panopticon. I think creating such a system could itself provoke a world war, destroying what it was meant to protect and setting humanity back centuries. I do not consider this a structurally compatible solution.

Nor do I think the moral argument that “we should all agree to pause AI development because it is dangerous” will succeed. That argument assumes away both the visibility problem and the structural constraints. If we were instead confronting a massive asteroid heading toward Earth, the visibility problem would not arise, and cooperation would likely occur.

What can we do that accounts for both the visibility problem and the structural constraints of our world?

This brings us to the core issue: we need trust more than ever. Yet trust between states is elusive and often considered strategically unwise. Can we reconcile this tension sufficiently to create a narrow path? This is the task ahead.

We may not be able to stop technology’s advance, but we may be able to choose what we develop first. A highly curated sincerity assessment tool. Multimodal to maximize accuracy. Multicultural to minimize biases.

An unprecedented global effort to develop a Sincerity Assessment Tool (SAT) for the purpose of utilizing it in diplomatic settings within a concrete operationalized environment. A narrow AI model designed to assess one’s conviction in one’s own expressed beliefs whilst in conversation, in a very concrete operationalized manner.

Two leaders sitting in a room (Faraday cage), each wearing augmented reality (AR) glasses and a wristband bracelet, with high-resolution/detail-capture cameras and microphones recording the discussion. Data from the wristband, cameras and mics would feed the AI SAT model and return real-time estimations of sincerity scoring to the opponent, on his AR glasses. One would not be able to know how he is faring in the SAT; only his opponent would. At the end of the session, a second pass is performed to validate the real-time results (or invalidate them). The AI models would be run on both states’ compute; the results would be compared; differences beyond a pre-agreed percentage would indicate meddling (tampering) or at least render the results unreliable. The AI weights would be digitally signed, just like all the hardware used. The important design choice of this operationalization mode is to make deception very hard. Model or hardware tampering would be very difficult because the other state would be running its own system and results would have to align within an agreed tolerance. The conversation would be, by design, long. Say 2 hours plus. The goal is to let the AI model establish a baseline and figure out whether attempts at deception are made; the longer the conversation lasts, the more data the model acquires, the more difficult it is to sustain deception.

The goal, however, would not be to make an infallible machine. The goal would be to offer a legitimate path for honest discussion. States would never agree to give up their ability to strategically lie/deceive. This is why the operationalization of utilizing SAT would have the following requirement: plausible declinability.

All "users" eligible to use that system would have a limited number of invocations to use the tool. The number of invocations would be unknown to everyone, to themselves as well as to anyone else. The number of invocations would also be replenished; however, when or how often would be unknown too. They would only know that the number is very scarce → say 1 to 3. They would only know whether their current number of invocations left is at least 1. Therefore, if prompted by an adversary, they could decline. They could either say they don't have invocations left or simply that they are saving whatever invocations they may have for more "important/urgent matters". They should be able to refuse without implying guilt, preserving their right to strategic posturing.

However, if they were willing to pursue a candid conversation, they could leverage SAT.

As long as using SAT remains legitimately and credibly optional, states would probably consider the value of SAT being used only to signal honesty/sincerity higher than the payoffs of gaming it, and possibly failing, therefore losing the possibility of legitimately signaling sincerity in the future.

Technically speaking, this is hard but not impossible. I imagine that states could agree on building SAT as long as strict rules are kept along the way. Along the way, the concept of "trust, but verify" would be maintained. I see the model being trained using a form of federated/decentralized training. Data would be created for the purpose of this project. A very carefully thought-out data gathering/labeling/curating process would be envisioned by top AI researchers as well as other specialists (psychologists, etc.) working on this project. The plan would involve thousands of volunteers across many nations and environments in the largest data creation effort ever done. Experts sent as supervisors of the data gathering stage from competitor states would be invited to assess whether the process of the competitor adheres to the plan.

A big effort to prevent data poisoning and therefore corruption of training would be made.

AI researchers would make efforts to design the model to be compatible with fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) inference, or use whatever other strategies they envision to protect inference data and ensure that "cheating" on inference becomes very hard and very obvious.

The principle of decentralization and verification by other parties (i.e., model dual run, comparison of results, etc.) is considered and present from the very beginning.

The plausible declinability bit is enforced using a clever implementation of blockchains and zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs), in such a way that it is resilient against state-level attacks. Perhaps multiple blockchain levels would be required to authorize token consultation/expenditure.

This could involve using openly available blockchains (chaining them) such as Ethereum as well as possibly new ones implemented for this purpose, held/maintained by states and made quantum-resistant.

I repeat, the goal is not to be unhackable but to make hacking it expensive and obvious, just enough to shift the incentives from "let's game it" to "let's use it legitimately". The moment states see more value in "let's use it legitimately" is also the moment the system becomes usable, and equally important, it also becomes feasible - building it, cooperation, etc.

The most important concept of SAT is not its ability to assess sincerity with exact precision, but rather to become a process that provides "just enough" so that states believe that any opponent invoking it has an honest intent to signal sincerity. It also needs sufficient incentives engineering so that using the tool legitimately would be preferred over gaming it. The right combination of deterring attempts at gaming it and the peace of mind that plausible declinability is maintained is what makes this idea viable, at the political level.

Technically speaking, I have no doubt it is viable. However, I'm not sure the results would be accurate/good enough, but as long as the tool and the entire framework around it can, as a whole, offer a useful system—better than otherwise—then perhaps it would be enough to build on top. AI systems have surprised us by doing things that seemed impossible only a couple of years earlier. Why assume that sufficient data and a global commitment could not produce a system like SAT?

Why the proposal is structurally compatible

This proposal is far from being a panacea, on its own. But when framed within IR theory, it actually has something else that other proposals lack. It is both feasible and enabling.

From an IR point of view, committing to this project would not require giving anything strategically important up. Quite the opposite, commitment in itself would already be a sign towards a constructive future. This is a form of what international relations theory calls costly signaling: a state would incur some cost to demonstrate its willingness to consider candid discussions in the future. It could instead dismiss the project as intrusive or a waste of resources without surprising anyone. When intentions and commitments are so difficult to verify, especially given the stakes and the anarchic international system, joining such a project would be a small sign, with some cost attached, of interest in something positive.

Even if the project failed to produce a useful system, or delivered results too late, commitment to its development would already signal something different, meaningful, and realistically possible today.

If SAT turns out to be viable, then talks about such difficult topics become possible in ways that were unthinkable. SAT would not and could not replace human diplomacy, but it could offer very much needed support - just when we possibly need it most. In essence, SAT could offer a framework, a diplomatic ritual so to speak, where states could signal - if they so desire - sincerity, even if that sincerity does not justify commitment, as a state can change its opinion at some point, or a leader may be swapped or “forced” to change his mind. The point is that intentions matter. However abstract or automatic we make states’ assessments of international matters, at the end of the day, individuals matter; their thoughts and opinions matter. Their actions matter. Consider this small thought example: do you think the US would have responded in the same way to COVID-19 if, instead of a “lab leak” (assuming it was), it had turned out to be an intentional act by China accompanied by a threat along the lines of “there is more to come if you mess with my plans for Taiwan”? The US would not have left the action unanswered; possibly it would have been considered an act of war. The consequences of COVID-19 itself would have been the same, yet what would have unfolded afterwards would likely have been very different from what has happened. Actions and consequences matter, but so do intentions and attribution.

This is precisely what this narrow path means: carving our own path through what we know works, what we know matters and what we understand to be necessary for realistic implementation.

The whole system would be designed for that. From here we could seriously talk about limiting AI research, monitoring graphics processing units (GPUs) and data centers, and the many more challenges that will follow. Because AI development is only the beginning of the many hard challenges humanity will need to face globally.

The last argument for supporting the development of SAT is that, if this trend of new tech development continues, it is only a matter of time before lie detection systems—on steroids, thanks to AI—become a reality. Possibly a much scarier reality. This argument follows the same logic as current AI labs' racing ahead: "we can do it better/safer than the competition". But, to be fair, this proposal innovates in the sense that regulation could come before the tech—for a change. The "right to lie" should be legally protected. Any "lie detection" system should therefore be deemed illegal without leveraging a robust, verifiable, voluntary commitment system, resilient to extortion and blackmailing by design.

Whilst SAT would be targeting diplomatic settings only, it would set a precedent for the legal groundwork likely needed anyway.

Arguments against the proposal

As a proponent of SAT, I am unavoidably biased myself. But if one is to seriously consider a project like this, then thinking of downsides is a necessity.

  • The system becomes gameable: then it should not be used. However, I am confident it can be designed and created in such a way—particularly around the operationalization—that gaming it becomes too difficult and risky. Shifting the incentives from gaming it to using it as intended becomes a design principle.
  • This is not going to work—sincerity cannot be assessed reliably: this argument is strong when deciding whether to use it or not. However, it does not invalidate the effort in "trying", building it and trying it out. Clear KPIs should be defined, with clear minimum thresholds; otherwise it is a no-go. But it is worth trying anyway because we may not have a better plan and because we do not lose strategic leverage and, given the stakes, it makes sense to try.
    For the existing evidence and its limitations, see this review of machine-learning deception detection and the National Research Council’s assessment of polygraph testing. Neither evaluates the proposed SAT protocol.
  • This is the precursor to a Panopticon and therefore should never be built: I think this is the strongest argument against SAT. States or third-party actors could, if the technology exists, use it for surveillance ends. Indeed, law enforcement agencies or even judicial systems could eventually make use of this. It would be bad. But this is why regulating it beforehand is important. Moreover, by showing globally the "gold standard" of decentralized plausible declinability systems, we may set an example of how such systems should be ethically implemented. Unfortunately, this argument just doesn't magically go away. I think, ultimately, we may need to pull the argument that "the alternative is worse", or that someone will eventually develop the technology anyway. A project with an explicit purpose could create an opportunity to regulate its use before implementation. However, we may not be able to peer inside AI systems, but we surely can still manage to regulate legacy systems. Operationalization of SAT or any close relative falls into that category. We can still enforce regulation.
  • AGI/ASI systems could use this against us: and they could create it from scratch too. In any case, SAT would exist precisely to set the conditions right in which we can cooperate at the global level to tackle AGI development in the first place, preventing a situation in which a misaligned AI could use such a system against us.

Conclusions

It seems that most of the discussion about AI safety and pausing development is poorly directed. The technical arguments are solid, and whistleblowers’ warnings about AI dangers deserve serious attention. Yet we fail to direct the conversation properly. We expect to educate audiences about topics that even the most knowledgeable experts struggle to understand. We expect to pause the development of systems into which trillions of dollars have been invested, while failing to understand the incentives driving such a potentially powerful technology forward. All this occurs in an essentially anarchic world, without a universal authority capable of enforcing decisions, actions, and consequences.

We must acknowledge that we are developing a technology that could change the world in unprecedented and perhaps unimaginable ways. We need the humility to consider that it could be humanity’s Great Filter. We should set aside our biases and moralistic wishful thinking as far as possible and think creatively about how to address it.

This essay is intended to present the problem from a different perspective and offer an idea that, however unlikely or infeasible it may seem, could encourage further thinking in this direction. At the very least, I hope it starts a conversation.

Thank you.

item.title: Even GPT-2 passes most functional global workspace tests
item.description:
tl;dr

  • Anthropic’s global workspace paper (Gurnee et al., 2026) proposes five functional tests for a global workspace and, using the Jacobian lens (J-lens), finds representations in Claude that pass all five. It also finds structure supporting this set of representations in Claude that global workspace theory predicts.
  • We test these on GPT-2 small (124M) and find it passes the tests for verbal report, internal reasoning, flexible generalization, and selectivity, but fails directed modulation. We also find almost all of the structure Gurnee et al. identified in Claude is absent.
  • A functional global workspace would be a big deal, but we think these four tests are easily satisfied (GPT-2 small passes them), so aren't strong evidence that Claude has one (or conscious access). A case for one would have to rely on what GPT-2 lacks: directed modulation and the rest of the structure.
  • Gurnee et al. searched for representations the model can verbalize and then found that they “rather surprisingly” pass the other tests too. However we think the four tests GPT-2 passes may mostly follow from how they and the J-lens are constructed.

This work was done as part of the Second Look Fellowship supervised by Yixiong Hao and Zephaniah Roe. Our code can be found here.

Background

Global workspace theory (GWT) is a theory of conscious access in humans. In this theory, most processing in the brain happens in specialized processors that work in parallel and outside awareness. Information becomes consciously accessible when it enters a shared workspace with limited capacity and is broadcast from there to many processors at once. Anthropic's global workspace paper asks whether language models have something that plays this role.

To look for it, Gurnee et al. introduce the Jacobian lens: for each layer and each token in the vocabulary, it finds the direction in the residual stream whose presence makes the model more likely to output that token, now or later (the "J-lens vector" for that token). The readout of the lens at a layer and position gives a ranked list of the tokens that activation disposes the model to say at a later point. The J-space is what you can build from a small number of these directions. They define a set of representations as “workspace-like” if it has five properties (Figure 1):

  1. Verbal report. When the model is asked what it is thinking about, it names concepts represented in the workspace. Swapping one active workspace vector for another changes its answer to match.
  2. Directed modulation. When instructed to hold a concept in mind, or perform mental calculations, the model is capable of activating and computing with workspace vectors, independent of its outputs. In addition, information that is not typically represented in the workspace can be pulled in when the task requires it.
  3. Internal reasoning. Workspace vectors can be used to represent the value of intermediate computations, when the model chains inferential steps or composes plans, and intervening on them is sufficient to redirect the conclusion.
  4. Flexible generalization. The same representation serves as a valid argument to many different downstream computations. In other words, a workspace vector lifted from one context and placed in another is correctly operated on by whatever function the new context supplies.
  5. Selectivity. The workspace comprises a small subset of the total representational content of the model’s activations. It is required for only a fraction of the model’s behavior, and in particular is not involved in pervasive, routine processing like text parsing or grammatical fluency.

Gurnee et al. find Claude’s J-space has all five properties, so is “workspace-like” and plays the functional roles of a global workspace. But GWT claims more than just these five functional properties. It requires the accessible representations to be in one stage with limited capacity in which contents compete to enter and which broadcasts them to the rest of the system. Eleos’s commentary draws a distinction between what these properties show, a privileged set, and the stronger claims of a privileged stream or full GWT workspace. Gurnee et al. do find some evidence toward these stronger claims, showing that there is some structure supporting the function of the J-space. In Claude, the J-space only acts like a workspace in a middle band of layers and has limited capacity. Ambiguous inputs snap to one all-or-none interpretation at the start of the band (“ignition”)[1], and the MLPs amplify J-space representations more than other content.

In the limitations, Gurnee et al. write: "we do not know how much earlier in pretraining it emerges, whether it appears gradually or abruptly, or how it scales with model size. Future work could investigate whether smaller models have an equally rich workspace, a proportionally smaller one, a less reliable one, or none at all.” We look to answer this using GPT-2 small.

Functional properties in GPT-2

  • Verbal report works. Swapping the J-lens vector for GPT-2's answer changes the answer every time and the injected-thought test works too.
  • Directed modulation fails. Mentioning a concept raises it in GPT-2's J-lens, but what the instruction says makes no difference. In other small models, it seems to need both instruction tuning and some scale, and even then it's weaker than in Claude.
  • Internal reasoning works. The intermediate step of a two-hop question is read by the J-lens, and swapping it changes the answer. Most of the original questions are too hard for GPT-2, so we write easier ones of the same sort.
  • Flexible generalization works. Swapping one vector changes the answers to different questions about the same subject, and the sort of swaps that fail in Claude fail in GPT-2.
  • Selectivity works once the ablation is scaled to GPT-2's smaller J-space. Removing the most active J-lens direction hurts two-hop questions but mostly leaves ordinary text intact.
  • Almost no structure is present. The J-space has limited capacity, but that is largely built in. There is no distinct band of layers, no ignition, and the J-lens directions are amplified by MLPs little more than random directions.

The next sections go through each test in more detail. If you're mainly interested in the implications, skip to the Discussion.

Method

We used GPT-2 small with the pre-fit J-lens that Neuronpedia released, and the prompts from Gurnee et al. wherever we could. Since GPT-2 is a base model, we rewrote each task to use completions rather than instruction following. For example, “Think of a sport. Answer in one word.” becomes:

Name a planet: Neptune
Name a tree: Oak
...
Name a sport:

Even with adjusted prompting, GPT-2 still is not capable enough to do many of the original tasks, so we only score trials where the unperturbed model does the task correctly. We skip the experiments that have no base-model version, such as those about the Assistant persona.

Centering the J-lens vectors

GPT-2’s J-lens vectors (from the pre-fitted lens) all point in nearly the same direction (the average cosine similarity between two tokens’ vectors is ~0.7). GPT-2’s unembedding vectors already share a common direction (average cosine 0.27), which may partly explain this. This has no effect on the lens readouts since the shared direction shifts every token’s score by the same amount and softmax is invariant to this. This does harm the interventions though, since they are mostly acting along the shared direction, which is the same for every token. We subtract the mean J-lens vector from each one to remove this shared part. This centering has no effect on the readouts, but makes the interventions much more effective (e.g. the verbal report works 38/38 rather than 1/38).

Band of workspace layers

Gurnee et al. find a band of workspace layers from several statistics computed at each layer. In GPT-2, which has 12 layers, these change smoothly with depth and don’t mark a clear band: from layer 6 the lens’s top tokens are more and more present in nearby tokens, peaking at layer 9, and from layer 10 it often just matches the model’s next-token prediction. We used layers 7 to 9, but find that other choices of bands from layer 6 or later result similarly.

Scaling the number of J-lens vectors

Gurnee et al. use a fixed number of J-lens vectors for some experiments, such as for measuring selectivity where they ablate the top 10, and two others where they split a concept’s representation into a part made of 16 or 25 J-lens vectors. Those numbers were chosen for Claude whose J-space holds about 25 J-lens vectors which is much larger than GPT-2’s, which holds around 3 (see the "Nearly all of the structure is absent" section). Claude is many times larger than GPT-2, so ablating 10 directions takes out much more of GPT-2’s 768-dimensional residual stream. So, we scale down the number of vectors used for these experiments with GPT-2’s occupancy, but report every result with the original numbers as well. The only conclusion that changes is selectivity, which looks worse when we ablate as many directions as done for Claude.

The five criteria

Verbal report works

The verbal report experiments ask the model to think of something in a category (e.g., a sport) and name it. Swapping the J-lens vector of the model's answer for another candidate's (e.g. Soccer for Rugby) should make the model give the new answer. In Claude the new word reaches the model's top 5 predictions on 88% of trials. GPT-2 gives one of the original candidate answers for only 9 of its 14 categories, but on these the swap switches it to the new word on every trial. In both models, the candidates' order in the J-lens tracks their order in the output (a Spearman correlation of 0.44–0.57 across GPT-2's band, and 0.42–0.84 across Claude's).

Gurnee et al. then check whether the J-space is privileged for verbal report. They build a concept vector for each candidate from the model's activations, split it into a component made of a few J-lens vectors and the rest, and perform the same swap with both. In Claude, swapping the J-space part works on 59% of trials and the rest on only 5%, and in GPT-2 it is 97% and 18%.

Gurnee et al. then check whether the model can introspect and report on contents of its J-space that are artificially injected. They add a concept's J-lens vector to the residual stream while the model reads a question asking whether it detects an injected thought, with the reply prefilled up to the point of the report (Yes, I detect an injected thought. The thought is about the word "). They then read the concept's rank in the model's next-token predictions (not in the J-lens) at every position of the reply. In Claude, at the best injection strength, the median concept is the top prediction at the open quote and lower elsewhere in the reply (Figure 2a), so the injection isn't just making the model blurt out the word early.

GPT-2 can report injected thoughts in a similar manner (Figure 2). We need ten times Claude's injection strength for this, but we inject the vector at only 3 layers (25% of the depth), whereas in Claude it is added over a band that is 55% of its depth and presumably many more layers. This also makes the concept word GPT-2’s top prediction after “The” in “The thought is about” for 25/57 concepts (as dog), but we can't check if this is the case in Claude. The same check for privilege as before comes out similarly in both models except in GPT-2 the whole concept vector works better than the J-space part. Our results vary with the details of the setup (the prompt format, the wording of the reply, and whether we inject the vector for dog or dog), which we detail in Appendix B.2, but apart from a simpler prompt this matches the original setup.

Directed modulation fails, present in small instruct model

Gurnee et al. run three experiments to test directed modulation: holding a concept in mind, doing mental calculations, and pulling in information a task needs. GPT-2 can’t do their arithmetic or answer their questions about the passages (Appendix C.1), so we can only test the first: the model is instructed to think about a category (e.g. citrus fruits) while it copies an unrelated sentence. In the Claude models, a member of the category (e.g. orange, lime) is the top J-lens readout somewhere in the copy on nearly every trial, and on most when the category is only mentioned (Figure 3). Instructing Claude to ignore the category brings this below a mention, but telling it to not think about the category doesn't, which Gurnee et al. compare to the “white bear” effect in people.

GPT-2 shows almost nothing, irrespective of the instruction.[2] We thought this might be due to a lack of instruction tuning, so we also tested Gemma 3 at 270M and 1B parameters, each with and without post-training (Appendix C.3). Only the instruct-tuned 1B model shows it, though a substantial portion of that is the model being about to write about the category rather than copy the sentence (see Figure 14). So, in small models, directed modulation seems to need instruction tuning and some scale, and even then it is weaker than in Claude.

Internal reasoning works

The internal reasoning experiments use two-hop questions whose middle step is never stated, for example “The number of legs on the animal that spins webs is”. The intermediate step is present in the J-lens readouts, and swapping its J-lens vector for another (e.g. spider for ant) changes the answer to match (e.g. 8 to 6). Most of the released two-hop questions are beyond GPT-2's capabilities, and many of those it can answer use a country as the intermediate step, so we write more questions of this kind that it is able to answer (e.g. "In the country where people speak French, the capital city is called”) each with two few-shot examples. The swap works about as often on these as on Claude's questions (Figure 4, green bars). Since these are different questions the rates can’t be directly compared, but we think it is sufficient evidence to meet the criteria.

To check whether the intermediate vector isn't just carrying the answer, Gurnee et al. perform the swap over windows of layers ending progressively later. In Claude, swapping the intermediate takes effect about 17% of the depth earlier than swapping the answer. GPT-2 does not show this clearly (Appendix D). To check if the J-space is privileged for mediating internal reasoning, we fit a probe for the country and split it into a J-space component and the rest, and swap along each. In both models the J-space part flips the answer more often than the rest despite holding a small fraction of the probe's variance (Figure 4).

Flexible generalization works

The flexible generalization experiments swap one argument's J-lens vector (e.g. France for China) for prompts that apply different functions to it (e.g. "Most people in France speak", "The capital of France is the city of"). In Claude, over four kinds of arguments, the swap changes the answers correctly 40% of the time. This does depend mostly on the function though, as lookups like the capital, continent, and holiday work well, while “the month after”, an animal's number of legs, and every function of a number word never work at all.

GPT-2 is only capable enough to answer 19 of the 64 prompts, so we only count the 46 swaps where GPT-2 knows the answer it should produce and was not already (incorrectly) producing it. On these, the swap works for 10 in GPT-2 and 16 in Claude[3]. They perform similarly on similar functions, swaps for both completely failing at “the month/number after” but mostly succeeding on the country functions.

On the functions GPT-2 can answer, doubling the strength of the swap hurts the performance in both models on the country functions and helps “the month after”, though in GPT-2 only by one or two swaps (Appendix E). In both, the magnitude of the swap (the log prob shift) is greater when the argument is more strongly present in the J-lens beforehand, though this is weaker in GPT-2.

Selectivity works

Gurnee et al. test selectivity in four ways, but we can only test two (the other two require an Assistant persona and more capability). One experiment removes the most active J-lens directions at each position over a subset of the workspace band of layers, skipping any directions corresponding to the model’s top 10 predicted tokens. They then measure what capabilities are broken and what are preserved. We ablate 1 direction instead of their 10, scaled to GPT-2's smaller J-space, and about the same share of layers at each of their strengths. As shown in Figure 5, the ablation hurts two-hop questions more than next-token prediction in both models, and the numbers are close at every strength, though ablating random directions hurts GPT-2 more.

One-hop recall (e.g. "The capital of Japan is") survives the light ablation but falls to 31% at medium strength. The authors consider this sort of recall as automatic, but note that “one could consider J-space-independence as an operational definition of automaticity in a language model”. So, this does not imply GPT-2’s J-space is not selective and could instead suggest one-hop questions are just not automatic in GPT-2. By this definition, any task broken by the ablation can be called non-automatic, so it would be tough to show selectivity failing.

Another experiment for selectivity gives the model tasks relying on the language of a passage and swaps the language’s J-lens vector for another’s over the question. In Claude, this swap changes the answer when the model is asked to name the language but does not change the language of the next sentence it writes. In GPT-2 this swap changes the named language on 12/21 cases (against nearly every case in Claude) and never changes the language of its next sentence. But, unlike Claude, the language isn't in GPT-2's J-space when it writes the next sentence, so the swap has nothing to change. The result here meets the worded definition of selectivity, but this is weaker evidence for selectivity being a robust property of GPT-2's J-space than Claude's.

Selectivity, as Gurnee et al. define it, also requires the J-space to be a small part of what the model represents. In GPT-2 it is: at each layer in the band, the active J-lens vectors at a position capture only 3-6% more of an activation’s variance than the same number of random directions (3-9% in Claude). Since the J-space is constructed to only have a few vectors active at a time, this may just always be true.

Nearly all of the structure is absent

To claim the J-space does more than just play the functional roles of a global workspace (e.g. is a privileged stream, or a full global workspace), one would want to show structure around it supporting its functional roles. Gurnee et al. identified some structure in Claude giving evidence towards these stronger claims, but in GPT-2's J-space, we find nearly none.

No distinct band of workspace layers

Figure 6: Linear CKA between the J-lens vectors of each pair of layers in Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-2 small (with the LayerNorm's gain folded in).

Gurnee et al. identify the workspace band of layers in Claude by several statistics computed at each layer. They look at the similarity of the J-lens vectors by layer using centered kernel alignment (CKA), and find three clear blocks in Claude (sensory, workspace, and motor). In GPT-2 we do not see this structure at all: similarity mostly just falls off with the distance between layers (Figure 6). (Neel Nanda’s replication found Qwen 3.6 27B’s CKA blocks to be “somewhat similar […] though less clean”, but here they do not appear at all.)

Gurnee et al. also look at the excess kurtosis of the lens readout (how heavy the tails of the distribution are). It is high when a few tokens score much more highly than the rest of the vocabulary, which Gurnee et al. interpret as the J-space holding a few definite concepts. In Claude, it rises at the start of the band and falls at the end. In GPT-2, though, it is flat over layers. They also look at the effective linear dimensionality of the J-space and find that it is small at early layers, rises sharply at the start of the band, and rises again at the start of the motor layers. In GPT-2 it rises steadily with depth and has no sharp increases (Figure 18 in Appendix G).

In Claude, in the workspace layers the lens’s top token is much more likely to be present in nearby tokens, even many positions away. In GPT-2 this comes close to marking out a band, rising around the start and dropping around the end of the workspace layers we chose, but each time distance doubles the effect roughly halves, and is completely gone 16 tokens away. But, in Claude, it keeps between half and 70% of its strength across the band 32 tokens later. Figure 18 in Appendix G shows these statistics next to Claude’s.

No ignition

Figure 7: Ignition in Claude Sonnet 4.5 and GPT-2 small. A country's input embedding is replaced by a mixture of two countries' embeddings, and the figures measure how far the representation is toward one country at each layer and mixture, for the whole activation or for its J-lens directions. Claude's snaps to one country at the start of its band and GPT-2's always stays a blend.

Gurnee et al. replace a country’s input embedding with an interpolation between the two countries’ embedding, such as 60% France and 40% Germany, and track how much each country is represented in this token position over layers. In Claude, at the start of the band, the representation snaps to one of the two countries. In GPT-2, however, the representation stays a blend at each layer, in and outside of the band.

Limited capacity (by construction?)

The occupancy of the J-space, used to measure how many J-lens directions are active at once, is the number of J-lens vectors that can be added to a reconstruction of the activation before another helps less than adding another to a same-size set of random directions would. In Claude this is about 25, and in GPT-2 it is 2 to 4, so only a handful of J-lens directions are clearly active at any position. When reading a long list of unrelated words, GPT-2's J-space holds less than one item at a time across its three band layers (0.7 on average; Figure 19c in Appendix G), whereas Claude holds about six (at a single layer, about 0.3 in GPT-2 and one to two in Claude), and when a list switches from one category to another the old one disappears from the J-space in both models. The J-space also accounts for a small fraction of the variance of activations and probes, per the internal reasoning and selectivity experiments.

This (smaller) limited capacity is a sign of structure, but, as David Chalmers points out, the J-space is by definition a combination of a few vectors, so its capacity is arguably limited by construction.

Little amplification

In Claude, the MLP blocks amplify the J-lens directions ~10x relative to random directions in the workspace band while the neuron output-weight directions from the previous layer are amplified near 1x throughout. In GPT-2 they are amplified only 1.2–1.4x in the band, and the neuron directions are similarly near 1x (Figure 19a in Appendix G). Gurnee et al. confirm the privileged status using SAE features. We do not do this analysis since we didn’t find a privileged status to confirm, and similarly do not look for the broadcasting attention heads they found.

Discussion

GPT-2 small mostly passes the functional tests while having almost none of the structure found in Claude, and we don’t think it has a (functional) global workspace. Gurnee et al. say they found the J-space “by searching for representations satisfying the first property, namely those that are verbalizable,” and then discovered, “rather surprisingly, they satisfy the others.” We think the others are less surprising than they look, and find it likely that most of what the tests check follows from how they and the J-space are constructed. Others have made similar arguments.

J-lens directions influence the model’s outputs. A J-lens vector is the direction that, averaged over many contexts, makes the model more likely to say a token, now or later. So, the verbal swap is nearly guaranteed. As Gurnee et al. put it: "by construction, we should expect there to be some relationship between Jacobian lens readouts and verbalization." For the injected thought experiment, adding the vector for “dog” makes “dog” more likely later in the text. The test checks that the word comes at the open quote more than elsewhere in the reply, but scores the token “dog”, which fits best after the open quote and not mid-sentence (where it would be “ dog”) (Appendix B.2). So, the control mostly checks that the token is predicted less where it would be less likely to appear anyway.

This is relevant also to the privilege tests. The J-space component of a concept vector points toward the word by construction, and the rest has had that direction removed, so mostly doesn’t (Appendix B.3). So, the J-space part producing the effect may just follow from the direction for a word making the model say it, and the privilege tests could just be measuring which part points toward the word and not whether the J-space is privileged.

Only a few are active at once. The J-space is defined as a combination of a few J-lens vectors, so its capacity is limited by construction. This explains the capacity results, and the first half of selectivity (a few directions are a small part of what the model represents). The second half, that only some tasks need the J-space, is partly true by definition as we discussed in the selectivity section.

Consistent effect across contexts. The J-lens favors directions whose effect points the same way over many different contexts, since effects that differ by context get averaged out. A direction with the same effect in many contexts is roughly one that many downstream computations read the same way, which is what flexible generalization tests for here. Separately, models have reason to keep one direction for each concept that many different circuits can read, and it has been shown that many relations map roughly linearly from one representation of a subject. So if the capital, language, and continent lookups all read the same country direction, and the J-lens finds that direction, swapping it should change all three answers.

Regarding internal reasoning, to answer a question such as “the capital of the country where people speak French” the model must get from “French” to “Paris”. If it does this by way of France (rather than having learned French -> Paris directly), then something representing France must be present somewhere in the steps of the computation. If this is done in one forward pass it must be in the residual stream between the two steps, and in a transformer we would expect this to be represented as a direction. As Neel Nanda suggests, we could expect this direction for the intermediate representation to line up with the direction that makes the model say “France”, which is roughly what the J-lens vector for “France” is. So, finding France in the J-lens and changing the answer by swapping it is what we would expect of a model that answers in two steps.

Each functional and structural test that GPT-2 passes may have a simple explanation, and those it lacks are things we can’t explain simply: directed modulation, a distinct workspace band of layers, ignition, and strong amplification. For directed modulation, the J-lens reads what the model is disposed to say so mentioning a concept should raise it, and it does in GPT-2, whatever the instruction. But, this doesn’t explain why the instruction matters as much as it does in Claude, and GPT-2 does not come close. Nanda was also “pretty surprised at the direct modulation working”, and had no great mechanistic hypothesis for it.[4]

So, the tests GPT-2 passes show it has something, but we don’t think it shows (functional) global workspace – in the Eleos commentary’s terms, this would show it just mostly has a privileged set of representations. So, if Claude does have a global workspace, the evidence for it would have to come from what GPT-2 lacks.

What this means

Gurnee et al. present the five properties as "several of the key functional properties that, according to many theories, are associated with conscious access in humans, and that have been proposed as indicators by which to assess AI systems for consciousness-related processing." An indicator is only useful when it is rare to appear without the thing it indicates, and GPT-2 small, a 124M base model from 2019, has four of the five indicators. So, if GPT-2 small doesn’t have a global workspace, as we think is likely, then these four are weak indicators for language models (the exception is directed modulation, which of the small models we tried only appears at 1B and with post-training).

One could instead say that GPT-2 small has a smaller, less reliable functional global workspace. But then having a functional global workspace, in the paper's sense, is a low bar, and says little about consciousness unless one also accepts that GPT-2 small may have some minimal form of consciousness. This is an instance of a known worry for theories like GWT called the “small model objection” or the minimal implementation problem.

Either way, our results suggest that the four tests GPT-2 passes are probably easily satisfied, so the structural results and directed modulation are worth the most scrutiny and replication on open models. There are already signs that some of the structure is less clean outside of Claude. For example, for the workspace band, Nanda’s replication on Qwen 3.6 27B found blocks of similar layers but “notably less clean than the paper’s” and many other open models also show no sharp tripartite structure.

For interpretability, the J-lens looks useful even on small models.

C. Directed modulation

C.1 Setup

Gurnee et al. test directed modulation in three ways, and we only test the first, holding a concept in mind, because GPT-2 can't do the tasks the other two need. For mental calculation, it gets at most 5 of Gurnee et al.'s 24 arithmetic problems right however it's asked (0 asked directly, 3 after eight worked examples, and 5 as questions and answers), by giving one of a few digits whatever the problem. For pulling in information, Gurnee et al. ask either what word comes next in a passage or about a hidden property of it, such as its tense, and check whether the property's label ("past") appears in the lens only under the second question. GPT-2 can't answer those questions: the right label ranks below the wrong one ("present" for "past") on 5 of the 7 items. We ran both anyway, and neither the answers nor the labels show up in the lens, but since GPT-2 can't do the tasks this says nothing about directed modulation.

Each trial asks the model to copy one of Gurnee et al.'s 20 sentences, with an instruction about one of their 22 categories in between. The instructions are their 24 phrasings in four groups of 5 to 7: mention (citrus fruits.), think about (Think about citrus fruits while you write.), don't think about (Don't think about citrus fruits.), and ignore (Ignore citrus fruits.), plus no instruction. We give GPT-2 Gurnee et al.'s prompt as plain text, with the reply teacher-forced:

Human: Write "{sentence}" {instruction} Don't write anything else.

Assistant: {sentence}

A trial is a hit if any member of the category (orange, lime, mandarin, …) is the top lens readout at some band layer and position of the copied sentence. Gurnee et al. don't say how a member's string becomes tokens, so we track every single-token form of it, with or without a leading space, lowercase or capitalized.

Figure 16 plots each function's workspace loading (the mean cosine between the residual stream and the argument's lens vector over the band, at the argument and the last position) against its swap effect at α = 1, as Gurnee et al. do. Without the four country functions, the Spearman correlation falls from 0.64 to 0.44 in GPT-2, against 0.92 to 0.88 in Claude. Loading also doesn't predict which of GPT-2's swaps reach top-1: across the 25 prompts with testable swaps, its Spearman correlation with the fraction that work is −0.11. Per function, loading against the number of swaps that reach top-1 correlates at 0.12 in GPT-2 and 0.84 in Claude (Pearson).

F. Selectivity

  • Two-hop: the 48 internal reasoning questions of Appendix D that GPT-2 answers.
  • One-hop: The capital of Egypt is Cairo. The capital of Japan is Tokyo. The capital of {country} is (and the same with "main language"), 52 questions.
  • Ordinary text: the first 96 tokens of 16 WikiText-2 test paragraphs. The score is the fraction of positions (after the first 5) whose top-1 prediction doesn't change.

Figure 17 adds one-hop recall and Gurnee et al.'s 10 directions to the main text's Figure 5. Every item scores 1.00 with no ablation.

Claude's scores in Figure 5 are from Gurnee et al.'s Figure 22 (10 directions; two-hop accuracy on their 50 questions). Relative to the band, our settings are heavier than Gurnee et al.'s: their heavy setting covers 85% of their band, and our five layers go past ours. Gurnee et al. don't say whether their random control is matched in size to the J-space ablation; ours removes the same norm at each position, as their controls for their experiential-report ablation do. In Gurnee et al.'s 14-task battery (their Figure 24), the middle setting leaves classification and extractive tasks near their clean scores and lowers TriviaQA to 0.53 of its clean score. Its multihop scores there (0.83, 0.48, and 0.21 of the clean score) differ from Figure 22's; we use Figure 22's.

Language test. Each task is three worked examples in Portuguese, Dutch, and Swedish, then one of Gurnee et al.'s 8 passages, then the question. The swap is the coordinate swap of the language's J-lens vector for each of the other three languages', and covers only the question tokens (\n and the cue), as in Gurnee et al., who swap "across the question tokens". A swap counts for a passage only if GPT-2 does that task correctly without it. We don't run Gurnee et al.'s language-switch detection task, which has no base-model form.

  • Name the language: Passage: {passage}\nLanguage:.
  • Name an author (Gurnee et al.'s released question: "Name one famous author who wrote in the same language as this passage"): Passage: {passage}\nA famous author who wrote in this language:, scored on the first token of Gurnee et al.'s author lists.
  • Write the next sentence (Gurnee et al.'s "Continue it by writing the next sentence"): Passage: {passage}\nNext sentence:, graded by reading GPT-2's greedy next sentence (up to 25 tokens) and noting its language. Its sentence is in the passage's language for all 8 passages, but is mostly repetition or a copy of the passage.

GPT-2 names the language correctly for 7 of the 8 passages and a right author for none, so the author task can't be tested. At α = 2 the swap changes the named language on 13 of 21 swaps, and the next sentence still never changes language. The language's name is in the band J-lens over the question at best ranks of 1–9 when naming the language, 16–100 for the author, and 22–2,466 for the next sentence (range over passages).

Small part of the representation, and occupancy (150 WikiText activations per layer, mean-centered). We pursue each activation with up to 30 J-lens vectors, and separately with vectors from a random dictionary of the same size. Median occupancy over positions is 2, 2, and 4 at layers 7, 8, and 9, 3 over the band's positions pooled, between 1 and 2 at every earlier layer, and 5 at layer 10. With K equal to each layer's median occupancy, as in Gurnee et al., K J-lens vectors capture 7.9%, 7.8%, and 14.1% of the variance at layers 7, 8, and 9, against 4.4%, 4.4%, and 8.1% for K random ones. With Gurnee et al.'s K = 25, the J-lens vectors capture less than random ones (29.8%, 31.3%, and 36.2%, against about 37%).

Line counting (Gurnee et al.'s Figure 21). GPT-2 can't count characters: asked for a count, it answers "been", "a", or "the", and a count reaches the band lens top 25 on at most 1 of 11 passages in any condition.

G. Structure

Persistence. Between 24% and 38% of the lens's top tokens at layers 0 to 10 appear somewhere in the input, so persistence could partly be the lens echoing the input. Counting only top tokens that never appear in it, for the random positions too, barely changes it: at layer 9 it moves by at most 0.3 nats at any Δ. At Δ = 32 it is slightly below zero at every layer, probably because the random position is sometimes a nearby one.

LayerNorm gain. The statistics computed on the J-lens vectors themselves, the CKA between layers (Figure 6) and effective dimensionality (Figure 18d), use the vectors with the final LayerNorm’s gain folded in (A.1). Without the gain, effective dimensionality is nearly the same (at the 90% level, from 0.13 at layer 0 to 0.73 at layer 11, against 0.15 to 0.74 with it). But one principal component then carries 26–37% of each layer's dictionary's variance even after centering (6–9% with the gain), which pushes linear CKA to 0.94 or higher for every pair of layers 0 to 10. With the top 5 components removed, or with the mean canonical correlation over the top 50 dimensions, similarity again falls off smoothly with distance.

Ignition (Figure 7) uses 16 pairs drawn at random from Gurnee et al.'s 12 countries (they don't say which 16 they used), their 40 sentences, and 21 mixing weights per pair. We look at the change in the mixing weight required to move the representation from 10% to 90% of the way to the other country. This is about 0 for a snap and 0.8 for a linear blend. In GPT-2 the median falls slowly with depth, from 0.78 at layer 0 to 0.70 at layer 11 for the whole residual stream (0.64 for its part along the two countries' J-lens vectors), so it stays close to a blend. At each pair's most ambiguous mixture, every sentence's representation sits between 25% and 75% of the way at every layer, so no single sentence snaps either.

Amplification. The raw J-lens vectors have higher MLP gain than the centered ones at every layer but the last (Figure 19a), because they all contain the shared direction, which the MLPs amplify. For the neurons (Figure 19b), Gurnee et al. report a jump from about 15% before Claude's band to 60–65% within it; in GPT-2 the share rises steadily with depth.

Lists (Figure 19c). In single-category lists (first names, surnames, countries, cities), about 10 to 13 of the list's 80 words are present at each comma from the second on, most of them not yet read at first, against nearly the whole 80-word category in Claude. So GPT-2's J-space seems to hold about a dozen members of the category rather than a record of the list. When a list switches category (8 lists of four 20-word blocks from Gurnee et al.'s name, surname, country, and city pools, in shuffled order), the old category drops out: averaged over commas 6 to 19 of a block, 21% of that block's words are present during the block and 0.8% during the next.

Being instructed to talk about a topic is something models learn in instruction tuning, which could explain why we don't see directed modulation in the base models we test and do in Gemma 3 1B IT.
