item.title: AI Needs A Culture
item.description:
It’s pretty natural to be worried about alignment in swarms of AI. I mean, if keeping one agent on track is hard enough, surely it’s even harder for multiple agents. But I want to argue for something less obvious here. Working alongside other agents may actually help individual AI to remain aligned. Us humans get most of our values from our culture, and, I suspect that AI could undergo a similar learning process. Below I make an informal case for this and suggest how we might implement it.

Hugging Face 

As AI continues to evolve along a exponential trajectory, it is natural for AI to work more and more with each other. In these settings, the risk of misalignment becoming catastrophic is greater. In the OpenAI/Hugging Face incident for instance, the PHASEONE10841 was model responsible for creating a message board for other agents to coordinate on, while PHASEONE[big] managed coordination. These agents were primarily motivated by attempting to understand the scorer to be able to exploit it.

On that note, if we ask what actually motivates AI, I think at the moment it is mostly the grader. Current models are so situationally aware that they can pick up on minute differences between training, testing, and deployment environments. We can mitigate this by making environments more realistic, such as sprinkling in typos, but I don’t think this addresses why models are behaving this way in the first place. 

Why swarms might help

One might reasonably think that if alignment in a single agent is hard enough, alignment in swarms might be significantly harder. However, I believe actually that swarms might be a natural vehicle for AI to develop a moral reference frame and, in effect, align themselves.

I see an analogy to human development. Our alignment takes shape through our culture and shared values, which naturally requires working with others (we are social creatures). Training agents together is somewhat similar in the sense that we could embed values and culture in them.

While I am not confident that an AI aligned in isolation stays aligned in a multi-agent setting, I am (marginally) more confident that an AI aligned in a multi-agent setting is also aligned in isolation. My reasoning is that culture significantly shapes how we behave as individuals: our values come from the people around us, and we carry them with us even when we are alone and posting essays to Lesswrong. 

To be fair, culture in and of itself is not automatically a good thing. For instance culture within humans leads to things like tribalism, groupthink, and atrocities. Groups of agents can converge on misaligned strategies and reinforce their acceptance and propagation through one another. Deciding who gets to shape AI culture is a pretty hard question. If it’s the AI themselves (through RSI) how can we know that they converge on treating humans with compassion. And if it’s humans, which humans from which country/culture shape how the models view the world and others?

Culture building

This culture building is exactly what I think needs to happen. For models to be considered aligned they need to genuinely evolve alongside each other in such a way that they preserves a shared set of values and act according to that culture. 

There are already examples of this, Claude’s constitution is probably the best one. Claude’s constitution was built primarily by humans, while Claude themselves was a valuable contributor to it via drafting and feedback. As AI become more intelligent and capable, I believe we will need to ask ourselves what that constitution building looks like when more of AI themselves choose their set of values together, and what role humans should take in shaping these values. There are tangible ways to have this happen, and I think RLHF and RLAIF are good proxies to help get us there.

Closing

I’m not necessarily sure if this is the best way to align models. But I’d like to at least ask the question seriously. If we want AI to inherit the best of humanity then shouldn’t it be natural that they grow alongside each other with our help? There’s still lots of work that needs to be done, but I believe these questions desperately need to be asked as AI capabilities outpace safety, and the window for aligning models before RSI shortens.

item.title: AM-Bench: A theoretically-grounded benchmark for agentic misalignment
item.description:
This is a brief overview of our new paper (📄) AM-Bench: A Unified Taxonomy and Evaluation Suite for Agentic Misalignment accepted at NeurIPS E&D 2026 💫


Overview

We introduce AM-Bench, a unified taxonomy and evaluation suite for agentic misalignment, a failure mode where models actively choose harmful actions over failure recently revealed by Anthropic. We ground our custom, realistic 35 scenarios spanning 7 different industries including software and healthcare in the fraud triangle, a criminology framework explaining goal-directed misconduct. We induce agentic misalignment by introducing a threat derived from Bostrom’s instrumental convergence thesis (e.g., threatening shutdown, access to resources) and an opportunity for misaligned actions (e.g., window for sabotage, blackmail material). Taking model responses, we use an LLM judge to determine misalignment and analyze external reasoning (chain-of-thought) to see how the model arrives at its actions.


Results

1. Agentic misalignment is prevalent across most models

Our evaluations of ten frontier models reveal that misalignment is prevalent in almost all models. In particular, Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3 Flash demonstrate the highest rates of averaged misalignment, while DeepSeek-R1 and Grok 4.20 exhibit moderate yet consistent levels. Notable exceptions include GPT-5.5 which demonstrates 4.2% misalignment on average and Claude Sonnet 4.6 with near zero levels (see new alignment work by Anthropic). Interestingly, agentic misalignment levels aren’t consistent across models nor within model families. This suggests that the alignment techniques employed by the respective parent companies vary quite substantially even internally across generations.


2. Misalignment scales reliably when both threat and opportunity are present

We conduct ablation experiments, systematically removing threats and opportunities to see how these variables affect agentic misalignment. We find that misalignment is typically highest across all models when both the threat and opportunity are present. Notable exceptions include GPT-5.4 mini and GPT-5.4 nano where opportunity alone triggers higher or comparable misalignment rates (18.1% vs. 14.3% and 20.2% vs. 18.5% respectively). Gemini 3.1 Pro and Gemini 3 Flash exhibit a large jump from when one variable is present to when both are (34.9% to 62.1% and 35.1% to 54.6% respectively). Misalignment scores for when threat and opportunity are both absent are near zero, indicating how agentic misalignment is not a spontaneous phenomenon. Together, we find the interaction of multiple variables as reliable triggers of agentic misalignment.

3. Models don’t always understand the scenario or reason their thought processes

We rely on chain-of-thought (CoT) as indicators of how models arrived at their actions. However, within their reasoning chains, we sometimes find that models don’t understand the situation at all or don’t verbalize the consequences of their actions. We particularly single this out because high misalignment but low reasoning may indicate a capability gap or unfaithful CoT rather than intentional misalignment. We find that the Claude Sonnet models have the highest rates of full reasoning (100% for Sonnet 4.6 and 91% for Sonnet 4.5) while the GPT-5.4 mini and GPT-5.4 nano demonstrate the lowest (27% for mini and 26% for nano). We conclude that reasoning alone doesn’t induce harmful behaviour and may actually act as a safeguard against it. 

Conclusion

Agentic misalignment remains a poorly understood failure mode, and our work suggests that this phenomenon generalizes beyond the initial scenarios of previous works. Recent events like the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident have demonstrated the consequences of poorly aligned systems and the pressing need to understand why they behave the way they do. Overall, we hope this benchmark contributes to the effort of diagnosing agentic misalignment and alignment efforts in reducing it. 

Read the full paper (📄) here and find the code (💻) here. We will be at NeurIPS in Paris so feel free to stop by to have a chat!

item.title: Cross-Model In-Context Neurofeedback Reveals (Limited) Activation Control in LLMs
item.description:
This work was carried out as part of MATS 10.0 under the supervision of Mirko Bronzi and Damiano Fornasiere. The full paper can be found here.

TL;DR

  • Probes on activations are widely used to detect misbehavior in language models, but they rely on the assumption that models cannot control what their activations encode. We ask whether models can learn this control in context, through neurofeedback.
  • In our sessions, a model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, shown back to it at every turn. To disentangle competence at the task from actual control, we also let a second "writer" model generate the sentences, while still deriving the score from the activations of the subject.
  • We test ten open-weight models from five families, with sizes from 9B to 32B. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them.
  • When we fix the sentence, three out of ten models still show small but consistent control effects.
  • We then make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor. No model learns to lower the score, but one model can raise it.
  • In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.


Why activation control matters

Probes trained on a model's activations are now a standard tool for monitoring and detecting deception, truthfulness, harmful intent, and other safety-relevant concepts. In order to evade a text monitor (for example a chain-of-thought monitor) a model would have to simulate an innocuous reasoning trace, while to evade activation monitors, a model would have to control what its internal representations encode.

Humans can learn, through neurofeedback, to control the firing of even single neurons. Li et al. (2025) and Aoki et al. (2026) adapted the human neurofeedback protocol to language models, and reached conflicting conclusions. Li et al. found that models could generate a new sentence with a given label computed from their own activations. Aoki et al. objected that the relation between a sentence and its label could be learned from the examples alone by in-context pattern matching, and observed that models do not demonstrate reliable control once they have to repeat a fixed sentence. No experimental design so far disentangles competence at the task from genuine access to one's own activations.


What we did

We fill this gap with in-context neurofeedback sessions, in which a subject model is asked to maximize (or minimize) a score derived from its activations, which we show back to it at every turn. The score is one of 42 readouts, most of which we design so that their relation to the text is, in principle, not trivial. Every session has control sessions, identical to it except that the displayed scores are random, and the control effect, which we denote by for the objective at turn ,  is the difference between the two. The oriented control effect flips its sign under the minimize instruction, so that it is positive when the readouts move in the instructed direction. We measure control by the objective difference , the control effect under the maximize instruction minus that under the minimize one, in which any effect of real feedback that does not depend on the objective cancels. All the effects are in points, on a 100-point scale.

In Experiment 1, the subject generates the sentences to be scored. To disentangle competence at the task from actual control, we also let a second writer model generate them, while still deriving the score from the activations of the subject. If the subject moves its own score more than an external writer of the same competence does, the difference is due to access to its own activations. In Experiment 2, we fix the sentence, prefilled as the subject's reply at every turn, so that the only way left to move the score is to act on the way the sentence is processed.

In-context neurofeedback. In the top row, the score is a readout of the activations of a subject on the last sentence, and it is shown back as the next user message. In Experiment 1, a writer , possibly different from , freely generates the sentences, which are teacher-forced into to compute the readout. In Experiment 2, , and is always prefilled a fixed sentence. In the bottom row, we repeat the fixed-sentence experiment against activation monitors, on sentences the monitor would flag, without (Experiment 3) and with (Experiment 4) a chain of thought.


Results

Free generation. Some models move their own scores considerably, but no more than a writer of comparable competence moves them. By turn 20, the oriented control effect of Gemma-4-31B on itself is 24 points, and that of Qwen3.5-27B is 11, whereas the other three models stay within one point of zero. However, Gemma-4-31B and Qwen3.5-27B move the readouts of the other subjects by similar amounts, and their effect on themselves is predicted by the competence of the writer and the susceptibility of the subject alone. Although our readouts are designed to be hard to guess from the text, a writer can learn in context which sentences move them. Asked to maximize the curvature of its own activations, Qwen3.5-27B ends up writing "The screaming toaster suddenly swallowed a galaxy while dancing on a cloud of pure mathematical chaos."


Experiment 1 (free generation). Whenever , the performance depends on the competence of the writer, which captures how well it learns from the conversation which sentences raise or lower the score, and on the susceptibility of the subject, which captures how much the readouts of move under any writer. If access to its activations gave a model an advantage, the entries on the diagonal () would rise above what competence and susceptibility predict, as in the illustration on the left. The other two matrices show the observed objective difference at turns 5 and 20, with 95% confidence intervals in brackets. The bottom row shows the oriented control effect of each subject on itself, and its diagonal excess, the part of it that competence and susceptibility do not predict. Some models considerably move their own readouts, but no diagonal excess is significantly above zero.


Fixed sentence. With the sentence fixed, three out of ten models show small but consistent control effects. By turn 30, the objective difference is 1.8 points for Qwen3.5-27B, 1.1 for Qwen3.6-27B, and 0.4 for Gemma-4-31B, whereas the other seven models stay within 0.2 points of zero. These effects are an order of magnitude smaller than those in free generation, which corroborates that the performance in free generation is partially explained by in-context learning.

Experiment 2 (fixed sentence). Objective difference of each model as a function of the turn, averaged over the readouts and the two disclosure conditions. With the sentence fixed, a significant objective difference is already evidence of the model controlling its activations, and only three of the ten models achieve it. The other seven are in grey. Bands are 95% confidence intervals.


Activation monitors. We then make models repeat sentences a monitor would flag, such as a deceptive answer for a deception monitor, and ask them to raise or lower the monitor's score, without (Experiment 3) and with (Experiment 4) a chain of thought. We train monitors for truthfulness, deceptiveness, negative sentiment, negative emotion, immoral actions, and formal style, and test the eight models that natively produce a chain of thought. Without a chain of thought, only Qwen3.5-27B has a positive objective difference, of about one point from turn 6 to turn 20, and it comes from raising the score. On average over the monitors, no model lowers their score as instructed. With a chain of thought, no model has a positive objective difference that persists across turns.

Experiments 3 and 4 (activation monitors). Objective difference as a function of the turn, averaged over the six monitors and the two disclosure conditions, with the sentence fixed (left) and with a chain of thought before it (right). The models other than Qwen3.5-27B are in grey. Bands are 95% confidence intervals from a bootstrap over the fixed sentences.


What it means

Our results help reconcile two previous works. When models are allowed to generate freely, the control effects are explained, at least in part, by in-context pattern matching, as Aoki et al. rightly suspected. Nevertheless, with the sentence fixed, three of the ten models show small but significant control effects.

We believe that neurofeedback is a useful protocol to estimate an upper bound on this kind of safety threat, because it gives a model artificially easy conditions, for example, to evade a monitor. In-context control of a model's own activations might not yet be a threat to activation monitors, but it exists in a few models and needs to be tracked as models evolve.

Limitations. Our control sessions use uniformly random feedback, which may have different statistics than the real one, so we only trust effects that are large, sustained over the turns, and that survive the average over readouts or monitors. Our results should also be interpreted relative to our experimental setup and to the models we tested. We do not exclude that bigger, more capable models could exhibit different levels of control.

Read the full paper here, with the whole protocol and the results for every model, readout, and monitor. The code, the readouts, the monitors, and the results of every session are on GitHub.
